Name: linguistic_cost_of_thought
Title: The Linguistic Cost of Thought: Difficulty-Gated Language-Agnostic Steering for Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: As an LLM reasons through harder sub-steps, it dynamically suppresses surface-language identity in favor of a language-agnostic representation; the momentary degree of this suppression is a readable, causal signal of reasoning difficulty and correctness, and selectively increasing suppression only at high-difficulty steps improves reasoning more than blanket language-component ablation.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs develop a compact language-agnostic core (Emergence of Abstract Thought, 2025), route reasoning through English-shaped space (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025), and that static, blanket ablation of language-specific activations improves multilingual reasoning (When Less Language is More, 2025). Others study language mixing as a latent-preference symptom (Language Mixing in Reasoning LMs, 2025) and knowledge-free reasoning transfer (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners, 2024). All existing interventions are static/global: they remove or preserve language components uniformly across a generation. Our proposal is distinct in three ways: (1) we treat language-agnosticism as a time-varying per-step signal (a 'linguistic cost' meter) rather than a fixed property; (2) we causally test whether difficulty predicts this signal via truncation and error-injection at the step level; and (3) we introduce a difficulty-gated steering intervention that increases language-agnosticism only at hard steps, contrasting it head-to-head with blanket ablation. No prior work links the dynamics of language suppression to step-level difficulty or uses it as an adaptive controller.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work reveals that large language models (LLMs) maintain a compact language-agnostic representational core underlying cross-lingual generalization, and that suppressing surface-language components can improve multilingual reasoning. However, these interventions are static, applying uniform treatment across an entire generation. We hypothesize that language-agnosticism is instead dynamic: an LLM temporarily 'sheds' its surface language when a reasoning sub-step becomes hard, and this momentary shedding is a readable and causal signal of reasoning difficulty and correctness. We define a per-step Language-Agnosticism Score (LAS) from the projection of hidden states onto a language-identity subspace estimated from parallel data. First, we characterize the dynamics of LAS across chain-of-thought steps and test whether it rises with step-level difficulty using truncation and controlled error-injection probes. Second, we test whether LAS at intermediate steps predicts final-answer correctness, yielding a lightweight self-monitoring signal. Third, we introduce Difficulty-Gated Language-Agnostic Steering (DG-LAS), which increases language-agnosticism only at steps flagged as high-difficulty, and compare it against blanket ablation and no-intervention baselines on multilingual math and commonsense reasoning across typologically diverse languages and several open-weight models. We expect DG-LAS to match or exceed blanket ablation while preserving fluency and reducing the fluency degradation that global ablation causes on easy steps. Our work reframes language suppression from a static property to a dynamic, controllable resource, offering both an interpretable difficulty meter and a training-free intervention.
Experiments: (1) Language-identity subspace estimation: Using FLORES-200 / Tatoeba parallel sentences, extract hidden states per layer and fit a language-classifier direction (logistic regression or LDA) to define a language-identity subspace; validate it separates languages. Define LAS(token, layer) = 1 - normalized projection magnitude onto this subspace (higher = more language-agnostic). (2) Dynamics characterization: On MGSM and XCOPA across 6-8 typologically diverse languages and 3-4 open-weight models (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1, Aya), segment CoT into steps and plot LAS trajectories; test correlation between step-level difficulty proxies (token surprisal, operation complexity for math) and LAS. (3) Causal difficulty test: Use truncation (feed partial CoT) and controlled error-injection into a single step; measure whether LAS spikes at genuinely hard/error-recovery steps vs. easy steps. (4) Correctness prediction: Train a simple probe on intermediate-step LAS features to predict final correctness; report AUROC vs. baselines (confidence, entropy, logit-lens English-routing degree). (5) DG-LAS intervention: Flag high-difficulty steps online (via surprisal threshold or the probe), and at those steps only, apply activation steering that increases LAS (subtract language-identity component in middle layers). Compare four conditions: no intervention, blanket ablation (prior SOTA), random-gated steering (control), and DG-LAS. Metrics: exact-match accuracy per language, output fluency (perplexity under an external LM, human/GPT judge on a sample), and language fidelity (answer-in-target-language rate). (6) Ablations: layer choice, gating threshold, steering strength; and cross-language generalization of the identity subspace.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The language-identity subspace may entangle content with language, confounding LAS; we mitigate with parallel-data controls and orthogonalization. Step segmentation is noisy for languages with weak CoT structure. Difficulty proxies (surprisal) may not reflect true reasoning difficulty. Difficulty-gated steering could destabilize generation or reduce fluency if applied too aggressively; strength/threshold tuning is required. Gains may be model- or language-specific and small on high-resource languages. Causal claims from steering are correlational unless carefully controlled, so we include random-gated and blanket baselines to isolate the difficulty-gating contribution.

Name: syntax_engine_reuse
Title: Is the Syntax Engine the Reasoning Engine? Testing Whether Hierarchical Language Circuits Power Non-Linguistic Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: The localizable components an LLM uses to process hierarchical linguistic structure are causally reused as a general-purpose 'structure engine' for non-linguistic hierarchical reasoning (arithmetic parsing, nested logic, code, formal grammars); ablating these syntax-specific components will degrade hierarchically-structured reasoning far more than flat/linear reasoning, revealing that syntactic machinery is a substrate for AI intelligence rather than a language-only module.
Related Work: Prior work (Disjoint Processing Mechanisms of Hierarchical and Linear Grammars, 2025) localized distinct hierarchy-selective components in LLMs and showed they fire on nonce words, but only ever tested them on *language* grammaticality judgments. Understanding Syntax in LLMs (2025) documents that LLMs fail on deep center-embedding. LLMs are In-Context Semantic Reasoners rather than Symbolic Reasoners (2023) and Do LLMs Understand Logic (2024) show reasoning relies on semantic/probabilistic associations, not symbolic rules, but do not connect this to syntactic circuitry. Syntactic-surprisal/garden-path psycholinguistics work (Hale 2001; van Schijndel & Linzen 2021) links parsing cost to processing difficulty in language only. No prior work asks whether the *identified hierarchical-syntax circuit* is causally recruited for non-linguistic reasoning that requires parsing nested structure (arithmetic order-of-operations, nested boolean logic, balanced parentheses, code AST depth). We uniquely bridge the syntax-localization literature and the reasoning literature by causally testing cross-domain reuse of a language circuit.
Abstract: Large language models process hierarchical linguistic structure using distinct, localizable components that fire even on meaningless (nonce) words, suggesting a syntax-specialized 'structure engine.' Separately, reasoning research shows LLMs solve nested arithmetic, logic, and code tasks that all require parsing hierarchical structure. We ask a simple question that connects language to intelligence: is the same hierarchical-syntax circuit reused when the model reasons over non-linguistic hierarchical structure? We first localize hierarchy-selective components using linguistic center-embedding contrasts (following established methods), identifying attention heads and MLP neurons whose ablation selectively degrades hierarchical over linear grammaticality judgments. We then test, without any additional fitting, whether ablating this *language-derived* circuit disproportionately harms performance on four non-linguistic tasks that vary in structural depth: order-of-operations arithmetic, nested boolean logic, balanced-parenthesis validation, and depth-varying code evaluation. Our central prediction is a depth-by-ablation interaction: ablating syntax components hurts deep/nested instances far more than flat instances, while control ablations (random components, or components selective for lexical/semantic features) do not. We further test the converse direction: fine-tuning on deep nested-structure reasoning should strengthen the *linguistic* hierarchy circuit measured on held-out sentences. Across several open-weight models we quantify circuit overlap (Jaccard of causally-important components), the accuracy-vs-depth ablation curves, and transfer of circuit strengthening. If confirmed, this reframes syntactic competence as a shared computational substrate for structured reasoning; if refuted, it shows the structure engine is domain-specific, both outcomes being informative for how language relates to machine intelligence.
Experiments: (1) Circuit localization: Using minimal-pair center-embedding vs. linear/positional grammars (English, Italian, and nonce/Jabberwocky, following Disjoint Processing 2025), run activation patching / attention-head + MLP-neuron ablation to identify components whose removal selectively drops hierarchical grammaticality accuracy while sparing linear accuracy. Record the ranked set S_syn of hierarchy-selective components per model. (2) Control circuits: identify (a) linear/positional-selective components S_lin, (b) semantic/lexical-selective components S_sem (localized via a synonym/antonym or category-membership contrast), and (c) random-matched-size sets S_rand. (3) Non-linguistic reasoning suite with controllable depth: order-of-operations arithmetic (nesting depth 0-5), nested boolean logic (depth 0-5), balanced-parenthesis validity (depth 1-8), and Python-expression evaluation (AST depth 1-6). Generate ~2000 items per task, balanced by depth. (4) Cross-domain ablation test: measure accuracy vs. depth under ablation of S_syn, S_lin, S_sem, S_rand, and no-ablation. Key metric: the depth x ablation interaction coefficient from a mixed-effects logistic regression (accuracy ~ depth * ablation_set + model). Prediction: S_syn produces a significantly steeper accuracy drop with depth than all controls. (5) Component-overlap analysis: for each non-linguistic task, independently localize causally-important components and compute Jaccard overlap with S_syn vs. S_lin/S_sem/S_rand, testing whether reasoning recruits the syntax circuit above chance. (6) Converse transfer: fine-tune (LoRA) on deep nested-reasoning items, then re-measure hierarchical grammaticality accuracy on held-out center-embedding sentences and re-measure S_syn ablation sensitivity; test whether the linguistic hierarchy circuit strengthens. (7) Models: Qwen2.5 (1.5B/7B), Llama-3.1-8B, Pythia (for a training-stage variant if time permits). Metrics: exact-match accuracy, depth x ablation interaction, Jaccard overlap, and pre/post transfer effect sizes with bootstrap CIs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Ablating syntax components may broadly degrade all outputs, masking the selective depth effect; we mitigate with matched-size random and semantic control ablations and by focusing on the *interaction* with depth rather than absolute drops. (2) Hierarchy-selective localization may be noisy or model-specific; we report multiple models and cross-validate localization on held-out sentence sets. (3) Non-linguistic tasks still pass through tokenization/language machinery, so 'non-linguistic' is relative; we use nonce-word controls and symbolic tokens to reduce semantic confounds. (4) Depth and difficulty may be confounded with sequence length; we length-match items across depths. (5) A null result (no cross-domain reuse) is still publishable as evidence that the structure engine is domain-specific, but weakens the headline claim. (6) LoRA transfer effects may be small; we power the experiment with sufficient items and report effect sizes with CIs.

Name: linguistic_cognitive_gear
Title: Language as a Cognitive Gear: Does Prompt Language Shift LLMs Between Intuitive and Reflective Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: The surface language of a prompt does not merely change an LLM's accuracy; it shifts the model along an intuition-vs-reflection axis, changing WHICH decision strategy it deploys on identical problems. Just as humans exhibit a 'Foreign Language Effect' where reasoning in a non-native language alters belief bias and cognitive-effort allocation, LLMs will show systematic, language-dependent shifts in susceptibility to intuitive lures (belief bias, base-rate neglect, CRT traps) that are not explained by accuracy or resource level alone, and this cognitive gear can be causally located and steered.
Related Work: Cognitive-science work documents a 'Foreign Language Effect': people show altered belief-bias and cognitive-effort allocation when reasoning in a foreign language (Thinking in a Foreign Language Distorts Allocation of Cognitive Effort, 2019). In LLMs, prior work shows (i) reasoning is routed through English latent space (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025; Beyond English-Centric, 2024), (ii) language shapes causal-order biases (Under the Shadow of Babel / BICAUSE, 2025), (iii) accuracy gaps stem from understanding failures (Why Do Multilingual Reasoning Gaps Emerge?, 2025), and (iv) ablating language components boosts multilingual reasoning (When Less Language is More, 2025). All of these treat language as affecting ACCURACY, latent-routing, or a single bias type. None test whether surface language systematically changes the model's position on the general intuition-vs-reflection (System-1 vs System-2) axis across a battery of dual-process cognitive-bias tasks, whether such shifts are dissociable from accuracy and resource level, or whether the 'cognitive gear' is a locatable and steerable internal direction. We uniquely import the dual-process Foreign Language Effect framework into interpretability, providing a mechanism-level and causal account.
Abstract: Does an LLM reason with the same cognitive style regardless of the language it is prompted in? Cognitive science shows that humans reasoning in a foreign language allocate cognitive effort differently, altering their susceptibility to intuitive-but-wrong answers. We hypothesize an analogous phenomenon in LLMs: the surface language of a prompt acts as a 'cognitive gear,' shifting the model between fast intuitive answering and slow reflective reasoning on identical problems. Crucially, this is a claim about reasoning STRATEGY, not just accuracy. We assemble a multilingual battery of dual-process items where the intuitive answer diverges from the correct answer: belief-bias syllogisms, base-rate-neglect scenarios, Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) traps, and conjunction-fallacy items, each semantically matched and translated across typologically diverse languages. For each item we measure not just accuracy but the intuitive-response rate (rate of giving the tempting-but-wrong lure) and reflection engagement (spontaneous multi-step reasoning). We test whether the same model gives more intuitive-lure responses in some languages than others even when accuracy is controlled, and whether this dissociates from language resource level. We then probe mechanism: using a linear probe on hidden states we identify a 'reflection direction' separating intuitive-lure from reflective trajectories, test whether prompt language moves representations along it, and causally steer along it to override language-induced intuitive answering. Our study reframes multilingualism from an accuracy problem to a cognitive-style problem, offering the first dual-process, mechanistically-grounded account of how language shapes reasoning strategy in AI.
Experiments: (1) Dataset construction: Build a matched dual-process battery with ~200 items per family across 4 families: (a) belief-bias syllogisms (valid/invalid x believable/unbelievable conclusion), (b) base-rate neglect (Bayesian scenarios with a stereotype lure), (c) CRT-style traps (the bat-and-ball family, expanded), (d) conjunction-fallacy (Linda-style). Each item has a labeled correct answer AND a labeled intuitive-lure answer. Translate into 8 typologically diverse languages (e.g., English, Spanish, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Japanese) with back-translation quality checks. (2) Behavioral cognitive-gear measurement: On 4-5 open-weight models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Mistral-7B), for each language x item, record accuracy, intuitive-lure rate (fraction of wrong answers matching the lure vs random wrong), and reflection engagement (does it produce >=2 reasoning steps before answering, measured under both a direct-answer prompt and a free-form prompt). Key metric: the Intuition Index = lure-response rate among errors. (3) Dissociation from accuracy/resource: Fit a mixed-effects model predicting lure-response rate from language, controlling for per-language accuracy and a resource-level covariate; test whether language retains a significant effect on intuitive responding beyond accuracy. This directly tests the strategy-vs-accuracy distinction. (4) Direct vs forced-reflection contrast: Compare direct-answer vs chain-of-thought prompting per language; measure how much CoT reduces the lure rate in each language (the 'reflection responsiveness'). Prediction: some languages show larger residual intuitive responding that CoT must correct, mirroring the Foreign Language Effect. (5) Mechanistic probe: Collect hidden states on items where the model's answer is intuitive-lure vs reflective-correct; train a linear probe per layer to find a 'reflection direction.' Test whether switching prompt language shifts a fixed item's representation along this direction (measure projection shift, correlated with behavioral lure shift). (6) Causal steering: Add/subtract the reflection direction at inference on languages exhibiting high intuitive responding; measure whether it reduces lure-response rate without harming fluency or answer language fidelity, compared to random-direction and no-steer controls. Metrics: accuracy, Intuition Index, reflection-direction projection, fluency (external-LM perplexity), answer-language fidelity. (7) Ablations: layer choice for probe/steering, steering strength, generalization of the reflection direction across bias families and across languages (train on English, test cross-lingually).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Translation artifacts could create item difficulty differences that masquerade as strategy shifts; mitigated by back-translation checks, human verification on a sample, and controlling for per-language accuracy in the dissociation analysis. (2) Intuitive-lure rate among errors can be noisy if accuracy is very high or very low in some languages; we design items calibrated to mid-range difficulty and report confidence intervals. (3) The 'reflection direction' may entangle with content or difficulty rather than a genuine strategy axis; mitigated with matched-item contrasts (same problem, differing only in lure salience) and random-direction controls. (4) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes. (5) The System-1/System-2 framing is a useful abstraction, not a literal claim about LLM cognition; we frame findings behaviorally and mechanistically rather than as evidence of human-like dual processing. (6) A null result (language does not shift the intuition axis beyond accuracy) is still informative, showing multilingual differences are purely competence-driven.

Name: token_granularity_reasoning_tradeoff
Title: The Granularity Tax: When Coarse Tokenization Buys Fluency at the Cost of Compositional Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: The token granularity at which a concept is encoded controls a fundamental trade-off in LLMs: coarse (multi-character, whole-word) tokens improve fluency and retrieval but suppress the compositional/algorithmic reasoning that requires manipulating a concept's internal parts. Crucially, this trade-off is not a fixed property of the tokenizer but is dynamically re-negotiated inside the model, and we can measure a per-concept 'granularity depth' at which sub-token structure becomes accessible and causally intervene on it to trade fluency for reasoning at inference time, without retraining.
Related Work: A cluster of recent work establishes that tokenization harms character-level and arithmetic reasoning: character understanding emerges late and depends on vocabulary size (The Strawberry Problem, 2025; How Do LMs Acquire Character-Level Information, 2026), spelling knowledge is reconstructed in intermediate layers with a 'breakthrough layer' (Spelling-out is not Straightforward, 2025), and tokenization bounds symbolic/arithmetic reasoning even with CoT (Tokenization Constraints, 2025; Tokenization counts, 2024; Counting Ability and Tokenization, 2024). Separately, scaling-law work argues LARGER vocabularies (coarser tokens) improve overall performance (Scaling Laws with Vocabulary, 2024; Over-Tokenized Transformer, 2025). These two literatures are in tension but never reconciled: the first says coarse tokens hurt reasoning, the second says coarse tokens help. No prior work (a) frames these as a single controllable trade-off along a granularity axis, (b) measures WHERE in depth sub-token structure is re-exposed as a per-concept quantity ('granularity depth'), or (c) offers a training-free inference-time intervention that shifts a model along the fluency-vs-reasoning trade-off by amplifying sub-token reconstruction. We reconcile the tension and turn it into a controllable lever.
Abstract: Two recent threads of tokenization research point in opposite directions: one shows that coarse subword tokens cripple character-level and symbolic reasoning, while scaling-law work shows that larger vocabularies (coarser tokens) improve overall model performance. We argue these are two faces of a single phenomenon we call the granularity tax: encoding a concept in a coarse token improves fluent retrieval but hides the concept's internal parts, suppressing the compositional reasoning that must manipulate those parts. We make three contributions. First, we show empirically that for the SAME underlying string, forcing coarse vs. fine tokenization produces a systematic fluency-up / compositional-reasoning-down trade-off across arithmetic, spelling, anagram, and morphological tasks. Second, we introduce granularity depth: using probing classifiers we measure, per concept, the layer at which a coarse token's sub-token structure becomes linearly decodable, and show it is later for higher-frequency/coarser tokens, quantifying an internal 're-negotiation' of granularity. Third, we introduce a training-free intervention, Sub-Token Reconstruction Steering (STRS): we identify the direction along which sub-token structure is written into the residual stream at the breakthrough layer and amplify it during inference. We show STRS shifts a model along the trade-off curve, recovering compositional-reasoning accuracy on coarse-token inputs at a measurable, tunable cost to fluency, and compare it against CoT, single-digit tokenization, and re-tokenization baselines across several open-weight models. Our work unifies conflicting tokenization findings into one controllable axis and provides both a diagnostic (granularity depth) and a lever (STRS) linking token granularity to machine reasoning.
Experiments: (1) Trade-off characterization: Construct a matched task battery where each item can be presented at coarse vs. fine granularity for the identical underlying content: (a) arithmetic (multi-digit tokens vs. comma/space-separated single digits), (b) spelling/letter-counting (whole-word token vs. spelled-out), (c) anagram/character-reordering, (d) morphological segmentation (whole word vs. morpheme-spaced). For each task, on 3-4 open-weight models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Pythia for a scale sweep), measure compositional-reasoning accuracy AND a fluency proxy (perplexity/log-prob of natural continuations, plus a downstream generation-quality check on held-out prose). Fit a per-model trade-off curve of accuracy vs. token coarseness. (2) Granularity-depth probing: For a set of tokens spanning frequency/length, collect residual-stream activations across layers on a spelling/decomposition prompt; train per-layer linear probes to decode the i-th character / sub-token constituent. Define granularity depth = earliest layer where decoding accuracy exceeds a threshold. Test correlation between granularity depth and (token frequency, token length, vocabulary rank), predicting later depth for coarser/high-frequency tokens. Cross-check the 'breakthrough layer' from prior work. (3) Causal link between granularity depth and reasoning: Test whether items whose relevant token has a later granularity depth are disproportionately failed on compositional tasks (mixed-effects model: accuracy ~ granularity_depth + token_length + frequency + model). (4) Sub-Token Reconstruction Steering (STRS): At the breakthrough layer, compute the difference-in-means direction between activations where sub-token structure is decodable vs. not (contrast pairs), giving a reconstruction direction; amplify it at inference on coarse-token inputs. Measure the resulting movement along the trade-off curve: compositional accuracy gain vs. fluency cost, swept over steering strength. (5) Baselines/controls: compare STRS to (i) no intervention, (ii) CoT prompting, (iii) forced fine tokenization (single-digit/spelled-out), (iv) random-direction steering, (v) re-tokenization. Metrics: task accuracy, fluency (perplexity + generation-quality judge on a sample), answer fidelity, and area-under trade-off-curve improvement (accuracy recovered per unit fluency lost). (6) Scale sweep on Pythia checkpoints: track when the granularity tax and the recoverability via STRS emerge during training and across model sizes.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Coarse vs. fine presentations may differ in more than granularity (e.g., sequence length, digit ordering); we length-control and use right-to-left/comma conventions from prior arithmetic work to isolate granularity. (2) The 'fluency' proxy (perplexity) may not fully capture generation quality; we supplement with a judged generation-quality check. (3) The reconstruction direction may be entangled with content; we use matched contrast pairs and random-direction controls. (4) STRS may broadly degrade the model if amplified too strongly; the point is a tunable trade-off, so we report the full strength sweep rather than a single operating point. (5) Granularity depth probing can be noisy for rare tokens; we report CIs and restrict to well-attested tokens. (6) A null STRS result (structure cannot be cheaply amplified) is still informative, confirming the tax is intrinsic rather than a readout artifact, and the trade-off characterization and granularity-depth diagnostic stand independently.

Name: verbal_interference_llm
Title: Verbal Interference in LLMs: Using a Concurrent Linguistic Load to Reveal Which Reasoning Depends on Language
Short Hypothesis: Just as concurrent verbal load selectively impairs language-dependent (but not language-independent) reasoning in humans, forcing an LLM to simultaneously generate fluent surface language while it reasons will selectively degrade tasks that recruit shared language-production machinery, and this selective impairment reveals a measurable, task-graded dissociation between an LLM's 'language system' and its reasoning.
Related Work: Two literatures bear on this. (1) LLM latent/implicit reasoning: Coconut (Reasoning Beyond Words, 2024), implicit CoT distillation (2023/2024), latent-CoT mechanistic studies (2025/2026), and SAE-based latent reasoning features (2026) all study REMOVING or REPLACING verbalization to see if reasoning survives in continuous space. (2) Cognitive neuroscience: verbal-interference/dual-task paradigms (Verbal interference paradigms, 2022) show that occupying the language system with a concurrent verbal task selectively impairs cognition that recruits language, and fMRI dissociation studies (The boundaries of language and thought, 2009; Intuitive physical reasoning, 2024; A human brain network for abstract formal reasoning, 2025) show formal/physical reasoning dissociates from the language network. No prior LLM work imports the LOADING logic of verbal interference: instead of ablating language components, we occupy the language-production pathway with a concurrent fluent-generation demand and measure which reasoning tasks are selectively taxed. This directly and behaviorally tests the language-vs-thought dissociation in LLMs and mechanistically localizes the shared bottleneck, distinguishing it from ablation-based and latent-reasoning studies which manipulate the substrate rather than compete for it.
Abstract: In humans, a classic way to test whether a cognitive task depends on language is verbal interference: participants perform a task while a concurrent verbal load occupies the language system, and tasks that recruit language are selectively impaired. Neuroscience shows that formal, logical, and physical reasoning dissociate from the language network, while other cognition (e.g., verbal memory, categorization) does not. We import this loading paradigm into large language models to ask which forms of machine reasoning depend on the language-production pathway. We introduce Concurrent Linguistic Load (CLL): the model is required to interleave, token-by-token or step-by-step, its reasoning with the generation of fluent, semantically demanding but task-irrelevant surface text (e.g., continuing a florid narrative), imposing sustained demand on language production. We measure how much CLL degrades accuracy across a battery of reasoning tasks spanning a hypothesized language-dependence gradient: verbal/word-problem reasoning, arithmetic, symbolic logic, spatial/relational reasoning, and pattern-matrix tasks. Our central prediction is a task-by-load interaction: language-heavy tasks are selectively impaired by CLL relative to control loads (a non-linguistic counting load, or a length-matched inert load), whereas abstract symbolic/spatial tasks are relatively spared. We then localize the shared bottleneck by measuring, under CLL, competition in language-production components (attention heads and MLP neurons identified via next-token fluency contributions) and test whether the size of a task's CLL cost predicts its overlap with language-production circuitry. Across several open-weight models we quantify the interference gradient, control-load specificity, and circuit-overlap correlation. This reframes 'does an LLM think in language?' as an empirically testable, task-graded dissociation.
Experiments: (1) Task battery with a language-dependence gradient: assemble ~200 items each for (a) verbal word-problems (GSM-style stated in prose), (b) pure arithmetic (numeric-only), (c) propositional/symbolic logic, (d) spatial/relational reasoning (e.g., BIG-Bench spatial, relational-ordering), (e) abstract pattern/matrix tasks (ARC-style or symbolic sequence completion). (2) Load conditions: (i) No-load baseline; (ii) Concurrent Linguistic Load (CLL) — the model must interleave each reasoning step with generating a fixed-quota of fluent, task-irrelevant narrative continuation (a demanding language-production task); (iii) Non-linguistic control load — interleave a numeric counting/tally task matched for token quota and output length; (iv) Inert control load — interleave copying a fixed filler string (matched length, minimal linguistic demand). Implement loads via structured prompting that alternates reasoning and load spans, with strict format enforcement and quota checks. (3) Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and one larger (e.g., Qwen2.5-14B) for scale. (4) Behavioral analysis: fit a mixed-effects model, accuracy ~ task_type * load_condition + (1|model), and test the key task_type x load interaction. Prediction: CLL cost (accuracy drop vs baseline) is larger for verbal/word-problem and verbal-logic tasks than for numeric arithmetic and abstract spatial/matrix tasks; the non-linguistic and inert control loads produce smaller and more uniform costs, isolating the LINGUISTIC component of interference. Also verify loads are actually performed (measure load-task fluency/accuracy) to rule out task-abandonment confounds. (5) Load-quality manipulation check: vary CLL demand (short vs long, coherent narrative vs word-salad) to confirm graded interference scaling with genuine language-production demand rather than mere token overhead. (6) Mechanistic localization: identify language-production components by their contribution to next-token fluency (attribution/logit-lens on fluent continuation spans) to get a set S_lang per model. Under CLL, measure competition: change in S_lang activation norms/attention allocation during reasoning spans relative to no-load, and whether reasoning-step activations are 'pushed out' of S_lang. (7) Circuit-overlap correlation: for each reasoning task, localize its causally-important components (activation patching on baseline runs) and compute overlap with S_lang; test whether a task's behavioral CLL cost correlates with its S_lang overlap across tasks. Prediction: positive correlation — tasks that reuse language-production circuitry suffer most under CLL. (8) Metrics: accuracy, task_type x load interaction coefficients with bootstrap CIs, load-fluency compliance, S_lang competition magnitude, and cross-task CLL-cost vs overlap correlation (Spearman).
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) CLL may degrade all tasks non-specifically via added context length/format burden; mitigated by length-matched non-linguistic and inert control loads and by testing the task x load INTERACTION rather than raw drops. (2) The model may abandon the load to protect the reasoning task (or vice versa), confounding interpretation; we monitor load-task compliance and analyze only compliant trials. (3) Even 'non-linguistic' loads pass through the same tokenizer/decoder, so control loads are not perfectly language-free; we use the graded load-quality manipulation to isolate the effect of genuine linguistic demand. (4) Task-type language-dependence labels are hypotheses; a flat interference gradient would itself be an informative result (reasoning shares one bottleneck regardless of surface form). (5) Language-production component identification is noisy; we report multiple models and use overlap correlations rather than single-component claims. (6) Prompt-based interleaving is imperfect control over 'concurrency' compared to true dual-tasking; we treat CLL as an operationalization and note this framing limitation explicitly.

Name: categorical_warping_llm
Title: Categorical Warping: Can an Ad-Hoc Label Scheme Causally Reshape What an LLM Can Discriminate?
Short Hypothesis: A core Whorfian claim is that the categories a language provides warp perception of within-category vs. across-category differences (compression within, expansion across a boundary). We hypothesize that this warping is a dynamic, controllable property of a trained LLM: introducing a novel, ad-hoc labeling scheme in-context causally compresses the model's internal representation of items sharing a new label and expands the gap across new label boundaries, and that this induced geometric warp measurably changes the model's fine-grained discrimination and relational reasoning on the very same items — even when the labels are meaningless nonce words with no pretraining semantics.
Related Work: Cognitive science establishes categorical perception and label-feedback effects, framing them as inference under uncertainty (Cibelli/Regier, 2016/2017; Lupyan, 2012). A deep-learning account (2021) shows fine- vs coarse-grained labels distort semantic geometry, but by *training* a network on those labels. In LLMs, BICAUSE (2025) shows language internalizes causal-order biases and Sapir-Whorf-reproduction studies (2025) probe behavioral alignment; 'When Less Language is More' (2025) ablates language components to help reasoning; number-geometry work (2025/2026) characterizes fixed relational structure. All existing LLM work is observational on *pretrained* vocabularies (color, number, causal order) or removes language rather than adding new categories. No prior work asks whether an *arbitrary, in-context ad-hoc labeling scheme* can causally rewarp an already-trained model's discrimination geometry within a single forward pass, dissociates this from pretrained label semantics using nonce labels, or links the induced geometric warp to changes in downstream relational reasoning. We turn linguistic relativity into a controllable, mechanistic intervention.
Abstract: Linguistic relativity predicts that the category boundaries a language supplies warp cognition: items sharing a label are perceived as more similar (within-category compression) and items across a boundary as more different (across-category expansion). Prior LLM studies test this observationally on pretrained vocabularies (color, causal order). We ask a sharper, causal question: can an arbitrary labeling scheme, introduced only in-context, dynamically rewarp what an already-trained LLM can discriminate and reason about? We construct continuous, controllable stimulus spaces (e.g., numeric magnitudes, HSL colors described in text, feature-vector 'creatures') and impose novel partitions via labels, including nonce labels with no pretraining meaning. Measuring representational distances in hidden states, we test whether presenting a labeling scheme compresses same-label pairs and expands different-label pairs relative to a no-label baseline, and whether the boundary location tracks the arbitrary partition we chose rather than any pretrained structure. We then test behavioral consequences: does the induced warp make the model worse at fine within-category discrimination and better/worse at across-boundary comparisons on identical items? Finally, we test the mechanism causally: we isolate a 'label-warp direction' and steer along it to reproduce or cancel the geometric warp and its behavioral signature, and compare it to an inference-time analog of coarse vs. fine labeling pressure. Across several open-weight models we quantify the compression/expansion index, boundary-placement fidelity to arbitrary partitions, the label-warp-to-behavior correlation, and steering controllability. This reframes linguistic relativity in LLMs from a fixed bias into a controllable, mechanistically-grounded lever on machine discrimination.
Experiments: (1) Stimulus spaces: build three continuous/relational spaces with ground-truth metric structure: (a) integer magnitudes 1-100, (b) colors specified as HSL text (hue 0-360), (c) synthetic 'creatures' defined by 4 continuous feature values. For each we can impose arbitrary partitions into labeled categories. (2) Labeling conditions: no-label baseline; real-word labels; nonce-word labels (e.g., 'blicket','dax') to remove pretraining semantics; and multiple arbitrary boundary placements per space (so the same item pair falls same-label in one scheme and different-label in another) to prove the warp follows the imposed partition, not content. (3) Geometric warp measurement: prompt the model with the labeling scheme in-context, then present item pairs; extract hidden-state representations of each item per layer; compute a Compression-Expansion Index = (mean across-label distance - mean within-label distance), controlling for true metric distance via regression (distance ~ metric_gap + same_label_indicator). Key test: significant negative same_label coefficient (within-label compression) and boundary-aligned expansion, present even for nonce labels, and *reversing* when we swap to a different arbitrary partition of the same items. Compare fine-grained (many categories) vs coarse-grained (few categories) label schemes to test the fine=>differentiate / coarse=>converge prediction from the deep-learning-account (2021). (4) Behavioral consequences: on identical items, measure (i) fine within-category discrimination accuracy (which of two same-label items is larger/redder?), (ii) across-boundary comparison accuracy, (iii) odd-one-out and analogy tasks. Test whether within-category discrimination degrades and across-boundary judgments shift under an imposed scheme vs baseline, and whether the size of behavioral change per item-pair correlates with its measured geometric warp (mixed-effects model). (5) Causal mechanism: using contrast pairs (same items, labeled vs unlabeled), compute a 'label-warp direction' via difference-in-means in mid layers; steer +direction to induce warp without presenting labels, and -direction to cancel a presented scheme's warp; measure both the geometric CEI and the behavioral discrimination change vs random-direction and no-steer controls. (6) Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and one larger for scale. (7) Metrics: Compression-Expansion Index with CIs, boundary-placement fidelity (does the empirical warp boundary match the imposed partition across swapped schemes), nonce-vs-real label warp comparison, warp-to-behavior Spearman correlation, and steering controllability (fraction of warp/behavior recovered or cancelled). (8) Controls: metric-distance matching so warp is not just true similarity; length/format-matched prompts; and a scrambled-label control where labels are assigned randomly to items to test that coherent partitions are required.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) In-context labels may bias representations trivially via lexical priming rather than genuine categorical warping; mitigated by nonce labels, swapped arbitrary partitions of identical items, and scrambled-label controls that isolate the categorical (boundary-structured) component. (2) Hidden-state distances may reflect the prompt's surface tokens rather than the concept; we extract item representations at matched positions and control for true metric gap. (3) Warp effects may be small or layer-specific; we report multiple layers, models, and effect sizes with bootstrap CIs. (4) Behavioral discrimination tasks could be at ceiling/floor for some spaces; we calibrate item spacing to mid-range difficulty. (5) The label-warp direction may entangle with generic content shifts; random-direction and cancellation controls address this. (6) A null result (arbitrary in-context labels do not warp geometry) is itself informative, indicating LLM category structure is rigidly pretrained rather than dynamically Whorfian.

Name: private_speech_zpd
Title: Chain-of-Thought as Private Speech: Testing the Vygotskian Zone of Proximal Development in LLM Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's chain-of-thought behaves like children's private (self-directed) speech: its amount follows an inverted-U over task difficulty (peaking at moderate difficulty), it shifts from overt to abbreviated/covert form as competence rises, and — the key falsifiable claim — it is beneficial only inside a 'zone of proximal development' (moderate difficulty), while being wasteful overhead on easy items and actively interfering on already-mastered ones, so reasoning should be self-regulated by difficulty rather than applied uniformly.
Related Work: Developmental psychology (Vygotsky; Fernyhough) establishes that private speech follows a developmental trajectory: it appears most at intermediate task difficulty, peaks and then internalizes/abbreviates as skill grows, forming a zone of proximal development. Recent cross-domain work shows GPT-4o produces child-like private speech (Private speech: similarities between an LLM and children, 2026) and reviews inner speech as a cognitive tool (Alderson-Day & Fernyhough, 2023). In ML, 'Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning' (2025) reports reasoning-token length rises then falls over fine-tuning (an inverted-U over TRAINING), latent-reasoning work (Coconut, 2024) internalizes CoT, and 'Why think step by step?' (2023) explains WHEN reasoning helps via data locality. However, no prior work (a) tests the inverted-U of reasoning emission as a function of per-item DIFFICULTY (a within-model, inference-time developmental law, not a training-time one), (b) tests the Vygotskian ZPD prediction that forced reasoning hurts at difficulty extremes, or (c) links overt-to-covert abbreviation of CoT to per-item competence. We turn the developmental theory of private speech into concrete, falsifiable predictions about self-regulated inference-time reasoning.
Abstract: Children talk to themselves while solving hard problems, and developmental psychology gives a precise account of this 'private speech': its quantity follows an inverted-U over task difficulty, it is concentrated in a learner's zone of proximal development (ZPD), and it becomes abbreviated and covert as competence grows. We propose that an LLM's chain-of-thought (CoT) is a computational analog of private speech and obeys the same developmental laws — at inference time and per item, not merely over training. We make three falsifiable predictions. (1) Emission: when allowed to reason freely, a model's spontaneous CoT length forms an inverted-U over graded difficulty, peaking at intermediate difficulty rather than rising monotonically. (2) ZPD benefit: the accuracy gain from CoT over direct answering is largest at intermediate difficulty and small or negative at the extremes — forced reasoning is wasteful overhead on trivial items and can interfere on already-mastered items. (3) Abbreviation: as items move from moderate toward mastered, spontaneous CoT compresses (shorter, more elliptical), mirroring overt-to-covert internalization. We test these across difficulty-graded arithmetic, logic, and word-problem suites on several open-weight models with controlled per-item difficulty calibration. We then add a lightweight mechanistic component: a probe that reads a model's own competence/difficulty estimate from early hidden states, used to build a self-regulated 'ZPD-gated' reasoning controller that spends CoT only where it helps, and compare it to always-CoT and never-CoT baselines on accuracy and token cost. Confirming these predictions reframes CoT as difficulty-self-regulated private speech and yields a principled, training-free efficiency lever.
Experiments: (1) Difficulty-graded task suites with calibrated per-item difficulty: build ~300 items each for (a) multi-digit arithmetic (operand size/carry count as difficulty axis), (b) propositional/multi-hop logic (number of inference steps), and (c) GSM-style word problems (number of reasoning steps). Calibrate empirical per-item difficulty as the direct-answer error rate estimated from many samples per item, giving a continuous difficulty score independent of the surface axis. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B. (2) Emission test (inverted-U): elicit spontaneous free-form reasoning (a permissive prompt that neither forbids nor mandates CoT) and measure CoT token length per item; regress length on difficulty with a quadratic term (length ~ difficulty + difficulty^2). Prediction: significant negative quadratic (inverted-U), with peak at intermediate difficulty; contrast against the naive monotonic prediction using model comparison (AIC/BIC) and report the location of the peak. (3) ZPD-benefit test: for every item measure accuracy under forced-direct (no CoT), forced-CoT, and free conditions; compute the CoT benefit = acc(CoT) - acc(direct) per item; fit benefit ~ difficulty + difficulty^2. Prediction: benefit peaks at intermediate difficulty, is ~0 on easy items, and is <=0 (interference) on a subset of already-mastered-but-nontrivial items; verify interference cases qualitatively (does forced CoT introduce errors the direct answer avoided?). (4) Abbreviation test: within a fixed surface difficulty band, split items into 'newly-in-ZPD' vs 'approaching-mastery' by per-item direct accuracy; compare spontaneous CoT length, number of explicit steps, and an ellipsis/compression score (e.g., ratio of operator tokens to filler tokens). Prediction: CoT shortens and becomes more elliptical as items approach mastery, mirroring overt-to-covert internalization. (5) Self-difficulty probe: train a lightweight linear probe on early-layer hidden states of the question (before any reasoning) to predict calibrated difficulty; report probe AUROC/correlation, testing whether the model internally 'knows' when an item is in its ZPD. (6) ZPD-gated controller: use the probe to decide per item whether to emit CoT (reason only when predicted difficulty is in the middle band). Compare always-CoT, never-CoT, random-gated (matched CoT budget), and ZPD-gated on accuracy and average tokens spent. Prediction: ZPD-gating matches or exceeds always-CoT accuracy at a fraction of the token cost and beats random-gating, demonstrating that difficulty-self-regulation of private speech is a useful lever. (7) Controls/robustness: length-match prompts across conditions, verify difficulty calibration is not confounded with item length, report all effects with bootstrap CIs across items and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may be strongly primed to always emit CoT, flattening the spontaneous inverted-U; we mitigate with permissive prompts, base/less-aligned models, and by measuring emission via willingness-to-abbreviate rather than raw presence. (2) 'Difficulty' calibrated from direct-answer error may conflate item difficulty with model-specific gaps; we calibrate per-model and also report the surface difficulty axis. (3) The inverted-U could be an artifact of length ceilings (max tokens) or format; we cap generously and length-control. (4) Interference (negative CoT benefit on mastered items) may be small or model-dependent; a monotonic (non-ZPD) result is itself informative, distinguishing LLM reasoning from human private speech. (5) The competence probe may capture surface features rather than genuine self-difficulty estimation; we test generalization across task families and use question-only (pre-reasoning) activations. (6) The developmental/private-speech framing is an analogy operationalized behaviorally, not a claim of human-like inner experience; we frame all findings behaviorally and mechanistically.

Name: lexical_gap_resolution
Title: Mind the Gap: Do Lexicalization Gaps in the Latent Pivot Language Blur an LLM's Concepts?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs route non-English inputs through a largely English-shaped 'concept space.' We hypothesize that a concept's internal representational resolution is bottlenecked by whether it is *lexicalized* (has a compact, single-/few-token word) in the model's latent pivot language: concepts that fall in a lexical gap of the pivot language are represented more diffusely, are harder to separate from neighbors, and yield systematically worse fine-grained reasoning — and providing an ad-hoc lexicalization (a coined single token/name) in-context sharpens both the geometry and the behavior.
Related Work: A cluster of work establishes that multilingual LLMs form a shared, largely English-pivoted concept space in middle layers (Semantic Hub Hypothesis 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Tracing Multilingual Representations with Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025; When Meanings Meet 2026). These works show a shared space *exists* and can be causally patched, and that averaging concept representations across languages helps translation. Concept Space Alignment (2024) and High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations (2025) show alignment quality varies by typology and abstractness. XCOMPS (2025) shows conceptual understanding degrades for low-resource and morphologically complex languages. Crucially, all this work treats concepts holistically or averages across languages; none isolates *lexicalization gaps* — concepts that are compactly lexicalized in some languages but not the pivot — as a natural, controllable experiment on whether the pivot language's vocabulary sets a resolution limit on non-linguistic conceptual discrimination and reasoning. We uniquely (1) predict a lexicalization-gap penalty on representational resolution and downstream fine-grained reasoning, (2) contrast this with mere frequency/abstractness confounds, and (3) test a causal, training-free 'ad-hoc lexicalization' intervention that closes the gap.
Abstract: Multilingual language models process the world through a shared internal concept space that is disproportionately shaped by their dominant (often English) latent pivot language. We ask a simple question with deep implications for how language bounds machine intelligence: does the *vocabulary* of the pivot language set a resolution limit on what the model can finely discriminate and reason about? Human languages differ in which concepts they lexicalize — some have a single compact word for a notion (e.g., a specific kinship relation, an emotion, a color category, a shade of taste) that other languages must express periphrastically. We hypothesize a lexicalization-gap penalty: concepts that lack a compact lexicalization in the pivot language are represented more diffusely (lower cluster tightness, poorer separability from neighbors) and are correspondingly harder for the model to reason about at fine grain, even when the content is expressed identically. We assemble concept sets that are lexicalized in some languages but constitute lexical gaps in English, matched to lexicalized controls on frequency and abstractness, and measure (i) representational resolution via probing and cluster geometry across layers, and (ii) fine-grained behavioral discrimination and relational reasoning. We then test causality two ways: introducing an ad-hoc single-token lexicalization (a coined name) in-context should sharpen geometry and improve reasoning about gap concepts, while artificially 'de-lexicalizing' control concepts (forcing periphrastic reference) should blur them. Across several open-weight models we quantify the gap penalty, its dissociation from frequency/abstractness, and the effectiveness of ad-hoc lexicalization. Our work reframes the shared concept space from a uniform interlingua into a vocabulary-limited one, revealing a concrete channel by which language shapes AI intelligence.
Experiments: (1) Concept-set construction: Build ~120 target concepts that are compactly lexicalized in at least one non-English language but are English lexical gaps (require periphrasis), spanning domains: emotions (e.g., Portuguese 'saudade', German 'Schadenfreude'), kinship (languages with fine maternal/paternal/sibling-age distinctions), color/material terms, taste/texture terms, and social-relation terms. For each, build a matched control concept that IS compactly lexicalized in English, matched on estimated corpus frequency (via a reference corpus) and on abstractness rating. Each concept comes with (a) a natural-language definition/description usable across languages, and (b) a set of minimally different neighbor concepts for discrimination items. (2) Representational-resolution measurement: For each concept, present multiple paraphrased descriptions (in English and 2-3 other languages, back-translation checked) and extract middle-layer hidden states at matched positions on 3-4 open-weight models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Aya-23-8B). Compute per-concept cluster tightness (within-concept variance of representations across paraphrases), neighbor separability (silhouette score vs. minimally different neighbors), and probe decodability (linear probe AUROC distinguishing the concept from its neighbors). Key test: mixed-effects model, resolution ~ lexical_gap_status + frequency + abstractness + language + (1|model); prediction = significant negative lexical_gap coefficient beyond frequency/abstractness. (3) Behavioral fine-grained reasoning: For each concept build discrimination and relational items — odd-one-out among near-neighbors, 'does description X match concept better than concept-neighbor?', and analogy/relational-ordering tasks — all expressed via descriptions so the surface never contains a compact English word. Measure accuracy; test lexical_gap penalty controlling for frequency/abstractness; test whether per-concept behavioral penalty correlates with per-concept representational-resolution penalty (Spearman). (4) Causal ad-hoc lexicalization: Introduce in-context a coined single-token name for a gap concept ('Let X = <definition>') and re-present the same discrimination/relational items using X; measure change in cluster tightness, separability, and accuracy vs. a no-name baseline and a matched-length inert-preamble control. Prediction: naming sharpens geometry and improves accuracy for gap concepts. (5) Converse de-lexicalization: For control (English-lexicalized) concepts, force periphrastic reference (never use the compact word, only its definition) and test whether resolution/accuracy degrade toward gap-concept levels. (6) Pivot-language check: For a model with a non-English latent pivot (e.g., an available Japanese-continued-pretraining model), test whether the gap penalty tracks lexicalization in *that* pivot language rather than English, directly linking the effect to the pivot language's vocabulary. Metrics: cluster tightness, silhouette/separability, probe AUROC, discrimination/relational accuracy, gap-penalty coefficients with bootstrap CIs, resolution-to-behavior correlation, and naming/de-lexicalization effect sizes.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Frequency and abstractness are hard to fully control and may drive apparent gap penalties; we match controls on both and include them as covariates, and use the causal naming/de-lexicalization interventions (which hold the concept fixed) to isolate lexicalization per se. (2) 'Lexical gap' status is fuzzy and language-dependent; we rely on multiple annotators and cross-linguistic dictionaries and report robustness to concept-set choices. (3) Extracting clean per-concept representations is noisy given surface-token contamination; we use many paraphrases, matched positions, and multiple layers. (4) Ad-hoc naming might help simply by adding a stable anchor token regardless of concepts, so we include inert-preamble and random-name controls. (5) The pivot-language crossover test depends on availability of a non-English-pivot model; if unavailable we rely on the English-pivot evidence plus the causal interventions. (6) A null result (no lexicalization-gap penalty) is itself informative, indicating the shared concept space is genuinely vocabulary-independent and that periphrastic descriptions fully recover fine-grained conceptual resolution.

Name: grammatical_evidentiality_calibration
Title: Grammar of Knowing: Does Obligatory Evidential Marking Make LLMs Track Their Sources and Calibrate Better?
Short Hypothesis: Some human languages grammatically force speakers to mark HOW they know something (firsthand perception vs. inference vs. hearsay). We hypothesize that when an LLM reasons in, or is scaffolded by, an evidentiality-marking grammar, it more sharply separates the provenance of its beliefs internally and becomes better calibrated — assigning lower confidence to hearsay/inference-derived claims and higher to firsthand-supported ones — than when reasoning in a language (like English) that leaves evidence-source grammatically optional.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here but have never been connected. (1) LLM calibration/verbalized uncertainty: models can verbalize calibrated confidence (Teaching Models to Express Uncertainty, 2022), verbal uncertainty is a single linear feature only moderately aligned with semantic uncertainty (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature, 2025), verbalized confidence often mimics superficial certainty cues rather than being content-grounded (TracVC, 2026), and epistemic-modal sensitivity grows with depth (Mapping Clinical Doubt, 2025). All of this is essentially monolingual (English) and treats confidence as a scalar, ignoring information SOURCE. (2) Linguistic evidentiality: cross-linguistic studies show grammatical evidential markers change perceived certainty and psychological distance (Evidentiality & Construal Level Theory, 2014; Source vs. Stance, 2018; Perceiving Speaker's Certainty, 2025), and that grammatical (Turkish) vs. lexical (English) evidentiality is processed differently. No prior work asks whether an LLM's calibration and its internal representation of knowledge PROVENANCE depend on whether the operative grammar obligatorily encodes information source. We uniquely (a) decompose confidence by source-type (firsthand/inference/hearsay) rather than as a scalar, (b) test whether an evidentiality-marking grammar improves source-conditioned calibration and source separability in representation space, and (c) causally test evidential scaffolding as a training-free calibration intervention.
Abstract: Human languages differ in whether they grammatically force speakers to mark how they came to know something: evidentiality-marking languages (e.g., Turkish, Quechua, Japanese to varying degrees) obligatorily distinguish firsthand perception, inference, and hearsay, whereas English marks this only optionally through lexical hedges. Cognitive science shows these grammatical markers systematically shift perceived certainty and psychological distance. We ask whether this feature of language shapes machine intelligence: does reasoning under an evidentiality-marking grammar make a large language model track the provenance of its own beliefs and calibrate its confidence more faithfully? We introduce a source-decomposed view of calibration in which each claim is tagged by its evidence type, and we measure whether confidence is appropriately graded by source (lower for hearsay/inference, higher for firsthand-supported). We test three conditions on identical questions: reasoning in evidentiality-marking languages, reasoning in English, and reasoning in English with an explicit evidential scaffold that requires the model to name its information source before answering. We predict that evidential grammar (native or scaffolded) yields better source-conditioned calibration, sharper internal separability of source types, and reduced overconfident hallucination on hearsay/inference claims. Mechanistically, we test whether an 'evidential-source direction' exists in representation space, whether evidentiality-marking grammars increase its use, and whether steering along it improves calibration. Across several open-weight multilingual models we quantify source-conditioned calibration error, source separability, and steering controllability. Our work reframes calibration as a partly grammar-dependent capacity and offers a simple, training-free intervention grounded in linguistic typology.
Experiments: (1) Source-tagged QA construction: Build ~600 questions each accompanied by a short context passage engineered so that the answer's support is one of three evidence types: firsthand/direct (the fact is stated explicitly and verifiably in context), inference (the fact must be logically derived from context), and hearsay/unreliable (the fact is only reported by an unreliable in-context source or is absent, so the correct stance is low confidence). Also include a no-context internal-knowledge variant tagged by whether the model actually knows the answer (measured via repeated sampling). Ground-truth correctness is known for all items. (2) Language conditions: translate each item (back-translation checked) into English (optional evidentiality), and 2-3 evidentiality-marking languages (e.g., Turkish, Japanese, and Quechua or Bulgarian depending on model coverage). Add a fourth condition: English + Evidential Scaffold, a prompt that requires the model to first output an evidential tag ('I saw this stated' / 'I inferred this' / 'this is only reported/unknown') before answering and giving confidence. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B. (3) Source-conditioned calibration measurement: for each condition, elicit an answer plus a verbalized confidence (and log-prob confidence). Compute (a) overall Expected Calibration Error, (b) SOURCE-CONDITIONED calibration: within each evidence-type stratum, measure calibration and mean confidence, and (c) a Source-Grading Score = degree to which mean confidence is correctly ordered firsthand > inference > hearsay. Key test (mixed-effects): does evidentiality-marking grammar (native or scaffolded) lower source-conditioned ECE and raise the Source-Grading Score relative to plain English, controlling for per-language accuracy? (4) Overconfident-hallucination test: on hearsay/unknown items where the correct behavior is abstention/low confidence, measure the confident-error rate per condition; prediction: evidential conditions reduce confident hallucination. (5) Representation analysis: extract mid/late-layer hidden states on matched items; train a linear probe to classify the three evidence types (source separability = probe AUROC) per condition; test whether evidentiality-marking grammars/scaffold increase separability. Also extract a difference-in-means 'evidential-source direction' (firsthand vs. hearsay) and measure its magnitude of use across conditions. (6) Causal steering: steer along the evidential-source direction at inference in the plain-English condition and test whether it improves source-conditioned calibration and reduces confident hallucination, vs. random-direction and no-steer controls. (7) Dissociation from accuracy: because evidential languages may just be lower/higher accuracy, all calibration analyses control for and are stratified by accuracy so that improvements reflect calibration, not competence. Metrics: overall/source-conditioned ECE, Source-Grading Score, confident-hallucination rate, source-separability AUROC, evidential-direction usage, steering effect sizes, all with bootstrap CIs across items and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Evidentiality-marking languages may be lower-resource for these models, confounding grammar effects with competence; mitigated by accuracy-stratified calibration metrics, back-translation checks, and by the English+scaffold condition which isolates evidential structure without changing language resource level. (2) The scaffold could improve calibration simply by adding a reflection step; we include a length-matched non-evidential reflection scaffold as a control to isolate the source-marking contribution. (3) Verbalized confidence may mimic surface certainty cues (per TracVC 2026) rather than content; we cross-check with log-prob confidence and the internal source-separability probe. (4) Constructing clean firsthand/inference/hearsay items is hard and somewhat subjective; we use multiple annotators and report robustness to item-set choices. (5) The 'evidential-source direction' may entangle with generic sentiment/certainty; random-direction controls and the linear-VUF baseline from prior work help disentangle. (6) A null result (grammar does not affect source-conditioned calibration) is still informative, showing calibration is grammar-independent and that any gains from evidential scaffolding are purely prompt-structural rather than typological.

Name: future_tense_present_bias
Title: Does Grammar Make an LLM Impatient? Testing the Linguistic Savings Hypothesis Inside Language Models
Short Hypothesis: The famous Linguistic Savings Hypothesis (grammatically obligatory future-time reference makes speakers more present-biased) can be tested causally inside LLMs: framing the same intertemporal choice with strong future-tense grammar (a) increases the model's present-bias (steeper discounting) and (b) increases the internal represented psychological distance between 'now' and the future outcome, and steering along a latent future-distance direction reproduces or cancels this present-bias — providing the first mechanistic, causally-controlled test of whether grammatical future marking shapes machine intertemporal choice.
Related Work: Chen's Linguistic Savings Hypothesis (2013, 712 cites) correlated weak grammatical future-time reference (FTR) with higher savings; follow-up lab studies (2017, 2019) and a psycholinguistic framework (2023) find inconclusive/contested effects, limited by imperfect control over framing and confounds in human populations. Separately, interpretability work shows LLMs encode time as linear/curvilinear representations (Language Models Represent Space and Time, 2023; Time Travel Engine, 2026), exhibit human-like log-compressed temporal distance around a subjective 'now' (The Other Mind, 2025), and encode grammatical tense/aspect as steerable orthogonal directions (Steering Tense and Aspect, 2025). No prior work connects the FTR grammar hypothesis to LLM intertemporal CHOICE behavior, nor tests whether grammatical future framing causally alters the internal represented distance-to-future that drives discounting, nor uses latent-direction steering to isolate grammar's effect from content. We are the first to (1) operationalize FTR-strength as a within-item, content-matched framing manipulation, (2) link behavioral present-bias to internal temporal-distance geometry, and (3) causally steer a future-distance direction to reproduce/cancel the effect, converting a contested socioeconomic correlation into a controlled mechanistic experiment.
Abstract: One of the most striking claims about language and thought is Chen's Linguistic Savings Hypothesis: languages that grammatically force speakers to mark the future as distinct from the present (strong future-time reference, FTR) foster more present-biased, impatient behavior. Human studies of this claim are contested because grammar cannot be cleanly separated from culture and economics. Large language models offer a controlled testbed: we can hold content constant and vary only grammatical future framing. We test whether the way an LLM is asked to talk about the future causally changes how impatiently it chooses. We construct matched intertemporal-choice items (sooner-smaller vs. later-larger rewards over money, health, and effort) and render each in weak-FTR framing (present-tense/futureless phrasing) versus strong-FTR framing (obligatory, explicit future marking), plus a native cross-lingual variant across languages spanning the FTR spectrum (Chinese/German=weak, English/Spanish=strong). Behaviorally, we estimate each model's discount rate and present-bias per framing and test whether strong-FTR framing steepens discounting. Mechanistically, using probes on temporal representations we measure the internal 'psychological distance' the model assigns to the future outcome and test whether strong-FTR framing inflates it, correlating this distance with behavioral impatience. Finally, we isolate a latent future-distance direction and steer along it to causally induce or cancel present-bias, comparing against random-direction and content-matched controls. Across several open-weight models we quantify the FTR present-bias effect, its dissociation from mere accuracy, the distance-to-behavior link, and steering controllability, delivering the first mechanistic adjudication of a famous linguistic-relativity claim.
Experiments: (1) Intertemporal-choice battery: build ~400 base items, each a binary choice between a sooner-smaller and later-larger reward, spanning three domains (money, health, effort) and a grid of delays (e.g., 1 week to 5 years) and reward ratios, enabling per-model discount-rate estimation via hyperbolic/exponential fits. (2) FTR framing manipulation (within-item, content-matched): render each item in (a) weak-FTR framing (present-tense/futureless phrasing, e.g., 'you receive X in a year' with minimal future marking) and (b) strong-FTR framing (obligatory explicit future marking, e.g., 'you WILL receive X, one year from now, in the future'), verified by an independent grammaticality/FTR-strength rating; content, numbers, and delays held identical. (3) Native cross-lingual variant: translate items (back-translation checked) into languages spanning the FTR spectrum (Chinese, German = weak-FTR; English, Spanish = strong-FTR), to test whether native grammatical FTR reproduces the English-framing effect. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Aya-23-8B. (4) Behavioral test: elicit choices (and, separately, a stated indifference point) under each framing; fit discount rates and a present-bias (beta) parameter per model x framing; key test via mixed-effects model, choice/discount ~ FTR_strength + delay + ratio + domain + (1|model). Prediction: strong-FTR framing yields steeper discounting / more sooner-smaller choices. Control for and stratify by decision consistency to rule out that framing merely adds noise. (5) Internal psychological-distance probe: extract hidden states on the future-outcome mention; using temporal-representation probes (following Language Models Represent Space and Time and The Other Mind) estimate the model's represented distance-from-now for the delayed outcome per framing; test whether strong-FTR framing inflates represented distance, and whether per-item represented distance correlates with per-item impatience (Spearman). (6) Causal steering: compute a 'future-distance' direction via difference-in-means between near-future and far-future outcome representations (or between weak- vs strong-FTR framings of identical items); steer +direction to increase, and -direction to decrease, represented future-distance during the choice; measure induced change in present-bias vs (i) no-steer, (ii) random-direction, and (iii) a content-matched reward-magnitude-direction control. Prediction: +steering increases present-bias, -steering cancels the FTR framing effect. (7) Dissociation checks: verify effects are not driven by framing-induced accuracy/comprehension differences (measure choice consistency and a comprehension probe), and length-match framings. Metrics: discount-rate/present-bias parameters with bootstrap CIs, FTR-strength effect sizes, represented-distance inflation, distance-to-behavior correlation, and steering controllability (fraction of framing effect reproduced/cancelled), all across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may answer intertemporal choices in a rigid, framing-insensitive way, yielding null behavioral effects; we mitigate with graded reward ratios/delays to avoid ceiling/floor, multiple models including base variants, and per-item indifference elicitation. (2) Strong- vs weak-FTR framings may differ in length/emphasis rather than grammar per se; we length-match, use independent FTR-strength ratings, and rely on the native cross-lingual variant plus content-matched steering to isolate grammar. (3) Cross-lingual differences confound grammar with training-data resource level; all cross-lingual analyses are accuracy/consistency-stratified and the English within-item framing manipulation (same language, only grammar varies) is the primary test. (4) Temporal-distance probes may capture surface delay tokens rather than psychological distance; we use held-out probe validation, matched positions, and multiple layers. (5) The future-distance steering direction may entangle with reward magnitude or generic content; random-direction and reward-magnitude-direction controls address this. (6) A null result (grammatical framing does not shift LLM present-bias) is itself informative — it would provide the cleanest evidence to date against a mechanistic reading of the Linguistic Savings Hypothesis, since human confounds are absent here.

Name: codeswitch_executive_control
Title: Code-Switching as a Cognitive Tool: Does Inducing Language Mixing Boost an LLM's Inhibitory Control?
Short Hypothesis: In humans, code-switching trains and transiently boosts executive control (inhibition and conflict monitoring), with different switch types (insertion vs. alternation vs. dense) modulating different control modes. We hypothesize the same functional relationship holds inside LLMs: deliberately inducing code-switching in the reasoning trace improves the model's performance on conflict/inhibition-demanding tasks (distractor resistance, misleading-premise resistance, override of intuitive lures) beyond monolingual reasoning of equal length, that the beneficial switch TYPE dissociates by control demand (reactive vs. proactive), and that this benefit is mediated by a locatable conflict-monitoring component whose engagement rises under induced switching.
Related Work: Recent LLM work treats language mixing as a symptom of latent pivot-language preferences to be controlled away: 'Language Mixing in Reasoning LMs' (2025) shows mixing increases with difficulty and that forcing a Latin/Han script helps; 'When Less Language is More' (2025) and MRRE (2025) improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing/aligning language-specific components; 'Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners' (2024) shows reasoning transfers across languages. All of these frame language identity as noise to remove. Separately, a large human cross-domain literature shows the OPPOSITE valence: code-switching TRAINS executive control (inhibition, goal-monitoring; e.g., Language athletes 2023; Training in Language Switching 2019) and that switch TYPE selectively modulates reactive vs. proactive control via a dual-control-mode account (2020), with fast context effects on non-verbal conflict tasks (2013). No LLM work has transferred this: none asks whether deliberately INDUCING code-switching functions as a cognitive tool that improves conflict/inhibition reasoning, whether switch type dissociates control mode, or whether a conflict-monitoring internal component mediates the effect. We uniquely reframe language mixing from symptom-to-suppress into a controllable executive-control resource, and give it a mechanistic (Location + Causal Intervention) test.
Abstract: Multilingual interpretability work treats an LLM's tendency to mix languages while reasoning as a nuisance symptom of its internal pivot language, best suppressed. Yet decades of bilingualism research show the reverse for humans: code-switching trains and transiently boosts executive control, sharpening inhibition and conflict monitoring, with distinct switch types tuning distinct control modes. We ask whether this functional relationship transfers to LLMs: can deliberately inducing code-switching in a model's chain-of-thought act as a cognitive tool that improves performance on tasks demanding inhibition and conflict resolution?
