We assemble a battery of conflict/inhibition-heavy reasoning tasks (linguistic-Stroop-style distractor items, misleading-premise math, cognitive-reflection lures, and irrelevant-context word problems) and compare monolingual reasoning against three induced switch regimes drawn from the psycholinguistic taxonomy: insertion (single foreign content words), alternation (whole-clause switches between languages), and dense switching (frequent intra-sentence switching). Crucially we control for confounds by matching reasoning length and adding a same-language 'switch-token' scramble control, so any gain reflects switching rather than extra tokens or translation. We predict induced switching improves conflict-resolution accuracy over length-matched monolingual reasoning, that alternation aids reactive (distractor) control while dense switching aids proactive (sustained-monitoring) control, mirroring the human dual-control dissociation, and that these gains dissociate from ordinary (non-conflict) reasoning. Mechanistically, we locate a conflict-monitoring direction/component (via probing on high- vs low-conflict trials) and test whether induced switching raises its engagement and whether steering it reproduces the switching benefit. Across several open-weight models we quantify the switching-benefit effect, its type-by-control-mode dissociation, and mechanistic mediation, reframing language mixing as a controllable executive-control resource.
Experiments: (1) Task battery emphasizing inhibition/conflict: (a) Linguistic-Stroop-style items where a salient distractor word/number must be suppressed to answer; (b) misleading-premise math (GSM-style problems seeded with a tempting irrelevant number that lures a wrong operation); (c) Cognitive-Reflection-Test lures (intuitive-but-wrong answer must be overridden); (d) irrelevant-context word problems (correct info embedded among distractor sentences). Build ~250 items per family, each with a labeled correct answer AND a labeled lure/distractor answer so we can measure lure-error rate, not just accuracy. Also include a matched NON-conflict control set (plain arithmetic/logic of equal surface difficulty) to test dissociation. (2) Reasoning regimes (all elicited via structured prompting with strict format enforcement): (i) Monolingual baseline (reason in prompt language); (ii) Insertion (translate key content words into a second language mid-reasoning); (iii) Alternation (switch entire reasoning clauses/steps between two languages); (iv) Dense switching (frequent intra-sentence switching every few tokens). Second language chosen per model from its strong languages (e.g., English<->Chinese, English<->Spanish). (3) Confound controls: length-match all regimes to the same reasoning-token budget; add a 'switch-token scramble' control that injects same-language filler/foreign-looking nonce tokens at the same positions as real switches (isolates switching from mere token perturbation); add a 'pure-translation' control (reason once fully in the second language) to separate switching from language choice. (4) Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Mistral-7B. (5) Behavioral analysis: mixed-effects model, accuracy (and lure-error rate) ~ regime * task_conflict_level + (1|model|item). Key test 1: induced switching (esp. alternation/dense) beats length-matched monolingual and both controls on CONFLICT tasks. Key test 2 (dissociation): the switching benefit is significantly larger on conflict tasks than on non-conflict controls (interaction), showing it is executive-control-specific, not a generic boost. (6) Switch-type x control-mode dissociation: classify each conflict task as reactive (transient single-distractor suppression: Stroop, CRT) vs proactive (sustained monitoring across distractor-laden context: irrelevant-context word problems). Test the predicted crossover: alternation helps reactive control most, dense switching helps proactive most (regime x control_mode interaction), mirroring the human dual-control-mode finding. (7) Mechanistic Location + Causal Intervention: (a) Location: on monolingual runs, contrast hidden states on high-conflict vs low-conflict/lure-resolved-vs-lure-failed trials and train a linear probe to find a 'conflict-monitoring' direction (report per-layer AUROC; validate on held-out items). (b) Mediation: measure whether induced switching raises the projection onto / activation of this direction during the critical resolution step vs monolingual, and whether per-item projection increase correlates with per-item accuracy gain (Spearman). (c) Causal test: steer +conflict-direction during monolingual reasoning and test whether it reproduces the switching benefit; steer -direction during dense-switch reasoning and test whether it cancels the benefit; compare against random-direction and no-steer controls (report sign, dose-response, and specificity: off-target non-conflict accuracy preserved). (8) Metrics: accuracy, lure-error rate, regime and interaction effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, control-mode crossover coefficients, conflict-direction probe AUROC, projection-to-benefit correlation, and steering mediation effect sizes. (9) Robustness: vary the second language (typologically near vs far), switch density, and format; verify switch compliance (that the model actually switches) to exclude non-compliance confounds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Induced switching may simply add tokens/'thinking time'; mitigated by strict length-matching, the switch-token scramble control, and testing the conflict-vs-non-conflict INTERACTION rather than raw gains. (2) Switching may degrade fluency or cause the model to lose the thread, hurting rather than helping; a null or negative result is still informative (it would show LLM language mixing is a symptom, not a tool, cleanly separating LLMs from the human executive-control literature). (3) The second-language choice confounds switching with translation quality; the pure-translation and random-direction controls plus multiple language pairs isolate switching per se. (4) The 'conflict-monitoring' direction may entangle with generic difficulty rather than genuine inhibition; mitigated by matched high/low-conflict contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering controls, and specificity checks on non-conflict tasks. (5) Reactive/proactive task labels are hypotheses; a flat (non-crossover) result would still test the core switching-benefit claim and is publishable. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) The human-cognition framing (executive control, dual control modes) is an operationalized analogy, not a claim of human-like cognition; all findings are framed behaviorally and mechanistically.

Name: answer_deferral_typology
Title: Think Verb-Last: Does Answer-Deferring Word Order Delay an LLM's Commitment and Reduce Premature-Answer Errors?
Short Hypothesis: Human psycholinguistics shows head-final (verb-late, SOV) languages defer the pivotal predicate, forcing the parser to keep multiple hypotheses open, whereas head-initial (SVO) languages front the verb and encourage early prediction. We hypothesize the same trade-off governs LLM reasoning: when a model reasons in (or is scaffolded into) an answer-deferring, verb-final structure, it commits to a final answer later in its chain-of-thought and keeps competing candidate answers alive longer, which reduces premature-commitment errors on problems that require revising an initially tempting wrong answer — and this delayed commitment is readable and steerable via an internal 'answer-commitment' direction.
Related Work: Human work shows head-initial SVO languages afford more prediction while head-final SOV languages rely on rich pre-verbal structure building and holding hypotheses open until the verb (Prediction in SVO and SOV, 2023; Hyper-active gap filling, 2015; Hindi verbal-prediction limits, 2021; Word order affects formulation time course, Tzeltal 2015). In LLMs, word-order studies focus on training-time inductive biases via synthetic/artificial languages (Ravfogel 2019; White & Cotterell 2021) or on representation of grammatical role (BERT word order, 2022) and incremental garden-path processing (2024). BICAUSE (2025) shows LLMs internalize language-specific causal-order attention biases. None of this connects word-order typology to WHEN an LLM commits to a reasoning answer, to whether verb-final/answer-deferring structure keeps its candidate-answer space open longer, or to premature-commitment errors on revision-requiring problems. We uniquely (1) transfer the human prediction-vs-deferral finding into LLM reasoning behavior, (2) operationalize word order as a within-item, content-matched reasoning-structure manipulation (answer-early vs answer-late), and (3) locate and causally steer an internal answer-commitment signal, distinguishing our claim from purely observational typology-bias work.
Abstract: Languages differ in where they place the verb: head-initial languages (English, SVO) front the predicate and let listeners predict early, while head-final languages (Japanese, Hindi, SOV) defer the verb, forcing the comprehender to keep multiple interpretations open until it arrives. We ask whether this typological trade-off shapes how large language models reason: does an answer-deferring, verb-final reasoning structure make a model commit to its answer later and hold competing candidate answers alive longer, thereby avoiding premature-commitment errors on problems that require overriding a tempting-but-wrong first guess? We construct reasoning items with a strong intuitive lure and manipulate, within-item and content-matched, whether the reasoning trace is structured answer-early (conclusion/predicate stated up front, then justified) versus answer-late (all evidence marshalled first, conclusion deferred to the end), plus a native cross-lingual variant across SVO and SOV languages. Behaviorally, we measure the token position of first answer commitment, the persistence of the lure answer as a live candidate across the trace (via next-token answer probabilities), and lure-error rate on revision-requiring vs. non-revision problems. We predict answer-late structure defers commitment, sustains multiple candidates longer, and selectively reduces lure errors where revision matters, while offering no benefit (or a cost) on problems where the first guess is correct. Mechanistically, we locate an 'answer-commitment' direction from hidden states contrasting pre- vs post-commitment steps, test whether answer-late structure lowers its early engagement, and steer it to delay or force commitment, causally reproducing or cancelling the behavioral effect. Across several open-weight models we quantify the commitment-timing effect, its revision-specificity, and steering controllability, reframing word-order typology as a controllable lever on reasoning commitment.
Experiments: (1) Task battery with intuitive lures and a revision axis: build ~250 items each for (a) misleading-premise math (a tempting irrelevant number lures a wrong operation), (b) Cognitive-Reflection-Test-style traps, (c) multi-hop logic where an early sub-conclusion is superseded by later evidence, and (d) belief-bias syllogisms. Each item has a labeled correct answer AND a labeled lure answer, and is tagged 'revision-requiring' (the intuitive first guess is wrong) vs 'non-revision' control (first guess is correct), so we can test selectivity. (2) Reasoning-structure manipulation (within-item, content-matched, via structured prompting with strict format enforcement): (i) Answer-early — state the tentative conclusion first, then justify (head-initial analog); (ii) Answer-late — marshal all evidence and defer the conclusion to the final token(s) (head-final/verb-last analog); (iii) Free baseline. Prompts are length-matched and use identical evidence content; only conclusion placement differs. (3) Native cross-lingual variant: translate items (back-translation checked) into SVO (English, Spanish) and SOV (Japanese, Hindi, Turkish) languages, testing whether native verb-final grammar reproduces the answer-late structural effect. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Mistral-7B. (4) Commitment-timing measurement: at each reasoning step, read the model's implicit answer via next-token/answer-slot probabilities for the correct vs lure candidate; define (a) first-commitment position = earliest step where the eventual answer's probability crosses a dominance threshold and stays, (b) candidate persistence = number of steps both correct and lure answers remain above a liveness threshold. Key test (mixed-effects): answer-late structure yields later first-commitment and longer candidate persistence than answer-early, controlling for trace length. (5) Behavioral selectivity: measure accuracy and lure-error rate per structure x revision-status; predicted interaction = answer-late reduces lure errors on revision-requiring items significantly more than on non-revision controls (executive benefit specific to problems needing revision), and may slightly hurt non-revision items (deferral cost). Test whether native SOV framing shows the same pattern, accuracy-stratified to separate structure effects from language-resource competence. (6) Mechanistic Location: contrast hidden states on pre-commitment vs post-commitment steps to fit an 'answer-commitment' direction (per-layer linear probe, held-out validated); test whether answer-late structure lowers early-trace projection onto this direction (delayed engagement) and whether per-item projection timing correlates with per-item first-commitment position. (7) Causal Intervention: steer -commitment-direction during answer-early reasoning to delay commitment (predict reduced lure errors on revision items), and steer +commitment-direction during answer-late reasoning to force early commitment (predict the benefit is cancelled); compare against random-direction and no-steer controls, reporting sign, dose-response, and specificity (non-revision accuracy preserved). (8) Metrics: first-commitment position, candidate persistence, accuracy, lure-error rate, structure x revision interaction effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, commitment-direction probe AUROC, projection-timing-to-behavior correlation, and steering controllability. (9) Robustness: verify structure compliance (that answer-late traces actually defer the conclusion), vary lure salience, and check trace-length matching to rule out a mere 'more thinking' confound.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Answer-late structure may simply give the model more evidence before answering (a 'more deliberation' effect) rather than a genuine deferral/open-hypothesis effect; mitigated by strict length/content matching, by testing the revision-specific interaction rather than raw accuracy, and by the native cross-lingual variant. (2) Instruction-tuned models may resist the imposed structure or emit the answer regardless of placement; we enforce format, verify structure compliance, and analyze only compliant trials. (3) Reading implicit commitment via answer-slot probabilities is approximate for free-form traces; we use constrained answer slots and multiple liveness thresholds, reporting robustness. (4) Cross-lingual SVO/SOV differences confound grammar with training-data resource level; the within-language answer-early/answer-late manipulation is the primary clean test and all cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified. (5) The commitment direction may entangle with generic confidence/difficulty rather than answer commitment per se; mitigated by matched pre/post-commitment contrasts, held-out validation, random-direction steering, and non-revision specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (word-order structure does not shift commitment timing or revision errors) is itself informative, indicating LLM reasoning commitment is independent of surface reasoning-order typology. (8) The head-initial/head-final framing is an operationalized analogy to human prediction-vs-deferral, not a claim of human-like parsing; findings are framed behaviorally and mechanistically.

Name: articulated_rule_repair
Title: Say-Do Gap: Can an LLM's Own Correctly-Articulated Rule Repair Its Rule-Violating Behavior?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs frequently state a linguistic or symbolic rule correctly (articulation) while violating that same rule during free generation (execution), and this say-do gap reflects a representational dissociation between an articulation pathway and an execution pathway rather than a lack of knowledge; therefore the model's own correctly-articulated rule can be causally injected into the execution stream to close the gap, improving compliance without external supervision.
Related Work: Prior work established the say-do / comprehension-competence gap only behaviorally and treats it as a limitation. Hu & Levy (2023) and Language Models Fail to Introspect (2025) show metalinguistic prompt responses diverge from and underperform direct probability measurements, concluding LLMs lack privileged self-access. Comprehension Without Competence (2025) frames a 'computational split-brain' where instruction and execution pathways are geometrically dissociated, and Large Language Models as Neurolinguistic Subjects (2024) distinguishes performance from competence. On the reasoning side, When Less Language is More (2025) and On Representational Dissociation of Language and Arithmetic (2025) show reasoning/arithmetic occupy regions separable from language. All of these DOCUMENT a gap or dissociation but none (a) test whether the articulation and execution pathways can be jointly located and causally manipulated, (b) ask whether the model's OWN correctly-articulated rule can be causally read out and injected to repair execution, or (c) turn the dissociation from a diagnosed weakness into a self-supervised, training-free repair intervention. We uniquely propose a Location + Causal Intervention account that converts a well-documented deficit into a controllable lever, distinguishing our work from purely descriptive introspection studies and from language-ablation reasoning work.
Abstract: Large language models routinely state a rule correctly yet break the very same rule when they generate freely: they will explain that a sentence should use the subjunctive, avoid a repeated word, respect an order-of-operations convention, or obey a stated constraint, and then produce output that violates it. Prior work documents this say-do gap and concludes that metalinguistic self-report should not be trusted as evidence of a model's generalizations. We take the opposite stance: if the model can articulate the correct rule, the knowledge exists somewhere in the network, and the failure is a dissociation between an articulation pathway (used when asked to state a rule) and an execution pathway (used when generating) rather than an absence of knowledge. We test three claims. First, the gap is real and graded: across linguistic (grammar, style, morphology) and symbolic (arithmetic conventions, format constraints) rule families, models articulate rules they systematically violate in generation, with a measurable say-do gap per rule. Second, articulation and execution are representationally dissociated: a probe can decode the correct rule from hidden states even on trials where the generated output violates it, and the components carrying articulation differ from those driving execution. Third, and most importantly, the dissociation is exploitable: we read out the model's own articulated-rule representation and inject it (via activation patching / steering) into the execution stream, causally increasing rule compliance without any external label or fine-tuning. We compare this self-supervised Articulated-Rule Repair against no-intervention, random-direction, and explicit-rule-prompting baselines across several open-weight models, reporting compliance gains, dose-response, specificity, and fluency cost. Confirming these claims reframes a diagnosed weakness of LLMs as a controllable bridge between what a model knows and what it does.
Experiments: (1) Rule battery with articulation and execution probes: assemble ~15 rules across families — (a) grammatical (subjunctive/agreement/negative-polarity from minimal-pair resources like BLiMP-style items), (b) stylistic/discourse (avoid repeating a specified word, maintain a required register), (c) morphological (produce a required inflection), (d) symbolic conventions (order-of-operations formatting, use of a specified numeral base or separator), (e) explicit instruction constraints (e.g., 'do not use the letter e', 'answer in exactly N words'). For each rule build (i) an ARTICULATION test: ask the model to state/judge the rule (grammaticality judgment or explicit rule statement, scored against ground truth), and (ii) an EXECUTION test: elicit free generation where the rule applies and automatically check compliance. Compute per-rule Say-Do Gap = articulation accuracy − execution compliance. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (2) Gap characterization: report the gap per rule and model, and test whether it grows with rule complexity / output length; confirm gaps exist even when articulation is near-ceiling (knowledge present, execution fails). (3) Location — representational dissociation: on execution trials, extract hidden states and train a linear probe to decode the correct rule / whether the rule is being satisfied, INCLUDING on trials whose final output violates the rule; high probe accuracy on violated trials shows the rule is internally represented yet not enacted (report per-layer AUROC). Separately localize (via activation patching) components that causally drive the articulation response vs. components that causally drive execution compliance; measure their overlap (Jaccard) to test dissociation. (4) Causal Intervention — Articulated-Rule Repair (ARR): (a) run the model on the ARTICULATION prompt and cache the hidden-state representation of the correctly-articulated rule (or compute a difference-in-means 'rule-active' direction from articulation-correct vs articulation-absent contexts); (b) during EXECUTION, inject this cached representation / steer along the rule direction at mid layers; (c) measure change in execution compliance. Key metric: compliance gain under ARR. (5) Baselines and controls: compare ARR against (i) no intervention, (ii) explicit-rule prompting (restate the rule in the generation prompt — the standard fix), (iii) random-direction steering, (iv) patching from an INCORRECT articulation (control that repair depends on the rule being correctly articulated), and (v) self-consistency (ask-then-generate in one prompt). Prediction: ARR closes a substantial fraction of the say-do gap, exceeding random-direction and matching or complementing explicit-rule prompting, and fails when the cached articulation was wrong (confirming it transfers the model's own knowledge, not a generic push). (6) Specificity and cost: verify ARR improves the target rule without harming off-target rules or general fluency (external-LM perplexity, task accuracy on unrelated items); report dose-response over steering strength. (7) Dissociation-to-repair link: test whether rules with larger probe-decodable-but-violated signal (bigger internal dissociation) benefit more from ARR (Spearman correlation across rules). Metrics throughout: articulation accuracy, execution compliance, say-do gap, probe AUROC, component overlap, ARR compliance gain with bootstrap CIs, specificity, and fluency cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The say-do gap may be small or near-zero for some rules once articulation is measured carefully; we include many rule families and report the distribution, and any rules with a genuine gap suffice for the repair test. (2) Articulation scoring can be noisy (open-ended rule statements); we favor forced-choice / minimal-pair articulation where possible and use automatic compliance checkers for execution. (3) The cached articulation representation may not be cleanly transferable across the articulation→execution context shift; we test difference-in-means directions as a more robust alternative and report both. (4) ARR could improve compliance simply by generic 'follow-the-rule' pressure rather than transferring the specific rule; the incorrect-articulation and random-direction controls isolate this. (5) Explicit-rule prompting is a strong, cheap baseline that may match ARR; a finding that ARR only matches it is still informative (it shows the gap is representational and closable internally), and ARR's value is in cases where the rule cannot be conveniently prompted (implicit/self-discovered rules). (6) Effects may be model- or rule-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes. (7) A null repair result is still publishable as evidence that the say-do gap reflects a deeper execution-pathway limitation (consistent with the 'architectural split-brain' hypothesis) rather than a retrievable-knowledge dissociation.

Name: iconic_naming_bootstrap
Title: Names That Help You Think: Does Sound-Symbolic Iconicity Bootstrap In-Context Learning and Referent Binding in LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Iconicity (sound-meaning congruence, e.g. 'kiki' for spiky) is not merely something LLMs passively recognize; it functions as a cognitive scaffold: when novel entities, variables, or categories are given iconic rather than arbitrary or anti-iconic names, an LLM learns them faster in-context, binds them to their referents more reliably, and makes fewer errors on downstream reasoning about them, and this facilitation is mediated by a locatable binding/association component whose engagement rises under iconic naming.
Related Work: A large recent cluster establishes that LLMs and VLMs can *recognize* sound symbolism: they exhibit bouba-kiki-like preferences (Kiki or Bouba?, 2023; With Ears to See, 2024; LEX-ICON, 2025; Adversarially Probing Cross-Family Sound Symbolism, 2025), can generate iconic pseudowords humans decode (Iconicity in LLMs, 2025), and encode iconicity as a psycholinguistic feature in embeddings (Word Meanings in Transformer LMs, 2025; Where meaning lives, 2026). Neuron-level work (Unveiling Language Competence Neurons, 2024) finds GPT-2-XL lacks specialized sound-shape neurons. Crucially, ALL of this treats iconicity as a perceptual/associative fact to be detected, never as an instrumental resource that changes reasoning or learning performance. Meanwhile human developmental science shows sound symbolism *facilitates* infant word learning (Miyazaki et al., 2013; Imai & Kita's sound-symbolism-bootstrapping hypothesis) and the physics-rooted account (2022) explains why iconic mappings are learnable. We are the first to transfer the bootstrapping hypothesis into LLMs: does iconic naming causally improve in-context learning, referent binding, and reasoning, and is there an internal binding mechanism that iconicity strengthens? This distinguishes us from all recognition-only prior work.
Abstract: Human infants learn words tagged with iconic sounds (round meanings for round-sounding words) faster than arbitrary ones, a phenomenon known as the sound-symbolism bootstrapping hypothesis. Large language models are known to *recognize* iconicity, but no work asks whether iconicity is functionally useful to them: does giving an LLM a sound-symbolically congruent name for a new entity help it actually learn and reason about that entity? We test whether iconic naming acts as a cognitive scaffold. We construct in-context learning and reasoning tasks in which novel entities, categories, or variables (defined only by their properties in context) are assigned names drawn from three regimes: iconic (name's phonology matches the entity's property, e.g. a spiky object named 'kikith'), arbitrary (phonologically neutral names), and anti-iconic (name mismatches the property, e.g. a spiky object named 'boumo'). Holding all content identical, we measure whether name regime changes (1) in-context learning speed (accuracy vs. number of examples), (2) referent-binding reliability (do models keep the right name attached to the right entity across a long context and under distractors), and (3) downstream reasoning accuracy about the entities. We predict an iconicity gradient: iconic > arbitrary > anti-iconic, with anti-iconic names causing systematic binding errors. Mechanistically, we locate a binding/association signal (via probing name-to-referent linkage in hidden states and attention) and test whether iconic naming increases its strength and whether steering it reproduces or cancels the naming benefit. Across several open-weight models we quantify the iconicity-facilitation effect, its dissociation from mere name memorability/length, and its mechanistic mediation, reframing iconicity from a recognized association into a controllable lever on machine learning and reasoning.
Experiments: (1) Iconicity-graded name banks: Using established phoneme-to-meaning mappings validated cross-linguistically (spectral-balance/temporal cues from Bouba-Kiki 2022; size symbolism from Adversarially Probing 2025; LEX-ICON dimensions), construct pseudoword names scored on target semantic dimensions: shape (spiky/round), size (big/small), speed, brightness. For each dimension build iconic, arbitrary (phonologically neutral, length-matched), and anti-iconic name sets; validate iconicity scores with an independent classifier and (on a sample) human ratings. (2) Task suite (content held constant across name regimes): (a) In-context category learning: novel categories defined by a property (e.g. 'spiky things vs round things') introduced via k labeled examples using pseudoword category names; measure classification accuracy vs. k (learning curve). (b) Referent binding: introduce N novel entities each with a property and a pseudoword name, then after filler/distractor context query 'which entity is X?' or 'what is the property of <name>?'; measure binding accuracy and mis-binding to phonological neighbors. (c) Downstream reasoning: multi-step problems (comparisons, sorting, relational inference) over the named entities where the property matters; measure accuracy. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (3) Core behavioral test (mixed-effects: outcome ~ name_regime + dimension + task + (1|model|item)): predict iconic > arbitrary > anti-iconic learning speed, binding reliability, and reasoning accuracy; predict anti-iconic names produce a systematic *cost* (below arbitrary), the strongest signature that phonology is being used, not ignored. (4) Confound controls: length-match and frequency-match names across regimes; add a 'scrambled-iconic' control (same phonemes, wrong dimension assignment) to isolate dimension-congruence from mere phoneme identity; add an orthographic-only vs. IPA-provided variant to test whether the effect survives tokenization; measure name memorability alone (recall of names without properties) to rule out that iconic names are just easier to remember. (5) Scale/emergence sweep: test on smaller models and Pythia checkpoints to see when iconicity-facilitation emerges. (6) Mechanistic Location: on binding trials, train a linear probe on hidden states to decode name->referent linkage (which entity a name is currently bound to) and measure per-layer AUROC; independently, measure name-token->entity-token attention as a binding signal. Test whether iconic naming yields higher probe-decodable binding and stronger binding attention than arbitrary, and whether anti-iconic naming *degrades* it. (7) Causal Intervention: compute a 'binding-strength' direction via difference-in-means between correctly-bound vs. mis-bound trials; steer +direction under arbitrary/anti-iconic naming to test whether it recovers the iconic-level benefit, and steer -direction under iconic naming to cancel it; compare against random-direction and no-steer controls, reporting sign, dose-response, and specificity (off-target reasoning preserved). (8) Mediation link: test whether per-item behavioral facilitation correlates with per-item binding-signal increase (Spearman). Metrics throughout: learning-curve slope/AUC, binding accuracy and mis-binding rate, reasoning accuracy, regime effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, probe AUROC, attention-binding magnitude, and steering effect sizes.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Iconicity effects may be washed out by tokenization (pseudowords split unpredictably), muting phonological signal; mitigated by testing IPA-provided variants, spelled-out phoneme forms, and multiple tokenizers/models, and by reporting whether any facilitation survives. (2) The effect could be pure memorability rather than binding facilitation; the name-recall-alone control and the anti-iconic *cost* prediction isolate genuine dimension-congruence effects. (3) Arbitrary/anti-iconic classification of pseudowords is imperfect; we use validated cross-linguistic mappings, an independent iconicity classifier, and human-rated samples, plus the scrambled-iconic control. (4) Instruction-tuned models may be robust binders, yielding ceiling effects that hide differences; we increase entity count, add distractors, and lengthen context to avoid ceiling. (5) The binding direction may entangle with generic difficulty; random-direction and specificity controls address this. (6) Effects may be small or model/dimension-specific; we test multiple models and dimensions and report effect sizes. (7) A null result (iconic naming gives no learning/reasoning advantage) is itself highly informative: it would show LLMs recognize iconicity but cannot *exploit* it as a learning scaffold, cleanly dissociating them from the human bootstrapping account. (8) The developmental bootstrapping framing is an operationalized analogy, not a claim of human-like acquisition; findings are framed behaviorally and mechanistically.

Name: counterfactual_marker_reasoning
Title: Mood Matters: Does a Grammatical Counterfactual Marker Unlock an LLM's Counterfactual Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: Bloom's contested claim that languages lacking a dedicated counterfactual/irrealis marker impair counterfactual reasoning can be tested cleanly inside LLMs: framing an identical problem with an explicit counterfactual mood marker (subjunctive/irrealis) versus an unmarked indicative causally improves the model's counterfactual reasoning and more strongly engages an internal 'irrealis mode' that keeps the actual world and the hypothetical world distinct; steering along this irrealis direction reproduces or cancels the marker's behavioral benefit.
Related Work: Bloom (1981) argued Chinese speakers reason counterfactually less because Chinese lacks a distinct subjunctive marker; this is contested (Exploring counterfactuals in English and Chinese, 2023, shows Chinese uses lexical/contextual cues). Recent LLM linguistic-relativity work is observational: BICAUSE (Under the Shadow of Babel, 2025) shows LLMs internalize language-specific causal-order attention biases; the Sapir-Whorf reproduction study (2025) probes behavioral alignment; grammatical-concept work (LLMs Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts, 2025; Naturalistic Causal Probing for Morpho-Syntax, 2022; A Geometric Notion of Causal Probing, 2023) shows number/gender/tense are shared, linearly-encoded, causally manipulable directions but never links a grammatical MOOD marker to a REASONING capability. My prior proposals covered evidentiality, future-tense present-bias, word-order commitment, and dual-process gears, but none address counterfactual/irrealis mood or counterfactual reasoning. This work is the first to (1) turn Bloom's famous counterfactual-marker claim into a controlled within-item grammatical manipulation in LLMs, (2) test whether the marker causally changes counterfactual-reasoning accuracy dissociated from language resource level, and (3) locate an 'irrealis mode' representation that separates actual from hypothetical worlds and steer it to reproduce/cancel the effect.
Abstract: A landmark and still-contested claim in the language-and-thought literature (Bloom, 1981) holds that speakers of languages lacking a dedicated counterfactual/irrealis marker reason counterfactually less readily than speakers of languages with an explicit subjunctive. Human tests are confounded by culture and education; large language models offer a clean testbed where content can be held fixed and only grammatical mood varied. We ask whether the presence of a counterfactual mood marker causally changes how well an LLM reasons about hypothetical, contrary-to-fact worlds. We construct counterfactual-reasoning items (contrary-to-fact conditionals requiring the model to compute what would follow in a hypothetical world without contaminating it with actual-world facts) and manipulate, within-item and content-matched, whether the antecedent is grammatically marked as counterfactual (subjunctive/irrealis) versus stated in unmarked indicative form, plus a native cross-lingual variant across strong-marker (English, Spanish) and weak-marker (Chinese, Indonesian) languages. Behaviorally, we measure counterfactual-reasoning accuracy and a diagnostic 'actual-world intrusion' error rate (importing real-world facts the hypothetical explicitly overrides). We predict the counterfactual marker improves accuracy and reduces intrusion errors, selectively on genuinely contrary-to-fact items. Mechanistically, we locate an 'irrealis mode' direction from hidden states contrasting counterfactual versus factual framings, test whether the marker increases its engagement and whether items with stronger engagement suffer fewer intrusions, and causally steer it: adding the direction under unmarked framing should recover the benefit, subtracting it under marked framing should cancel it. Across several open-weight models we quantify the marker effect, its dissociation from language resource level, and steering controllability, delivering the first mechanistic adjudication of Bloom's hypothesis.
Experiments: (1) Counterfactual-reasoning battery: build ~400 items, each a contrary-to-fact scenario followed by a question whose correct answer requires reasoning in the hypothetical world (e.g., 'A had property P; suppose instead A had property Q; what would follow?'). Each item is paired with a matched FACTUAL control (indicative, about the real world) and has (a) a labeled correct counterfactual answer and (b) a labeled 'actual-world intrusion' lure (the answer that would follow if the model reverts to real-world facts), so we can measure intrusion errors, not just accuracy. Include an 'already-true' subset where the hypothetical coincides with reality (no genuine contrary-to-fact demand) as a selectivity control. (2) Within-item mood manipulation (primary, clean test): render each counterfactual item in (i) MARKED form with an explicit counterfactual/subjunctive marker ('If A had been Q...', 'were A to be Q...') and (ii) UNMARKED indicative form conveying the same hypothetical content lexically ('Assume A is Q now; then...'), content, entities, and question held identical; verify marker strength with independent grammaticality ratings and length-match. (3) Cross-lingual variant (secondary): translate items (back-translation checked) into strong-marker (English, Spanish) and weak-marker (Chinese, Indonesian) languages, testing whether native marker availability tracks the within-language effect. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B. (4) Behavioral analysis (mixed-effects: accuracy/intrusion ~ mood_marker * item_type + (1|model|item)): predict MARKED framing raises counterfactual accuracy and lowers actual-world intrusion errors, selectively on genuinely contrary-to-fact items (marker x item_type interaction), with little effect on factual controls or already-true items. All cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified to separate the marker effect from language-resource competence; add a length-matched non-mood reflection preamble control to rule out that any 'extra structure' helps. (5) Location - irrealis mode: extract mid/late-layer hidden states on matched marked-vs-unmarked (and counterfactual-vs-factual) contrasts; train a linear probe to decode whether the model is in a hypothetical/irrealis mode (per-layer AUROC, held-out validated) and derive a difference-in-means 'irrealis direction'. Test whether the marker increases projection onto this direction and whether per-item irrealis engagement correlates (Spearman) with fewer intrusion errors. (6) Causal Intervention: steer +irrealis-direction during UNMARKED reasoning (predict recovered counterfactual accuracy / reduced intrusion) and steer -irrealis-direction during MARKED reasoning (predict canceled benefit); compare against random-direction and no-steer controls, reporting sign, dose-response, and specificity (factual-item accuracy and fluency preserved). (7) Metrics: counterfactual accuracy, actual-world intrusion rate, marker and interaction effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, irrealis-probe AUROC, engagement-to-intrusion correlation, and steering controllability (fraction of marker effect reproduced/cancelled). Robustness: verify marker compliance, vary marker construction, and check length matching to exclude a 'more deliberation' confound.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Unmarked indicative framings may still convey counterfactuality lexically well enough that the model reasons correctly, muting the marker effect; a null result is itself informative (it would provide the cleanest evidence to date AGAINST Bloom's mechanistic reading, since cultural confounds are absent) and we sharpen sensitivity with intrusion-error metrics and difficulty-calibrated items. (2) Cross-lingual differences confound grammar with training-data resource level; the within-language marked/unmarked manipulation is the primary clean test and cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified. (3) Marked vs unmarked forms may differ in length/emphasis rather than mood per se; we length-match, use independent marker-strength ratings, add a non-mood reflection control, and rely on content-matched steering to isolate mood. (4) The irrealis direction may entangle with generic difficulty or hedging rather than a genuine actual-vs-hypothetical world separation; mitigated by matched contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and factual-item specificity checks. (5) Instruction-tuned models may reason counterfactually robustly regardless of marking, yielding ceiling effects; we calibrate item difficulty, include harder multi-step hypotheticals, and test multiple models. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we report effect sizes with CIs across models. (7) Bloom's hypothesis framing is operationalized behaviorally/mechanistically, not as a claim about human-like cognition.

Name: metaphor_scaffold_reasoning
Title: Thinking Through the Concrete: Do LLMs Recruit Source-Domain Structure as a Scaffold for Abstract Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: When reasoning about an abstract target domain, an LLM recruits an internal representation of a concrete source domain (per Conceptual Metaphor Theory) and imports that source's relational/geometric structure into its inference; consequently, a metaphor whose source structure is ISOMORPHIC to the target's true structure causally improves abstract reasoning, while a structurally MISMATCHED source causally corrupts it, and this scaffold is a locatable, steerable internal signal rather than mere surface phrasing.
Related Work: Prior work shows metaphor knowledge is encoded in PLM middle layers (Metaphors in PLMs, 2022), that CMT-style prompting improves reasoning behaviorally (CMT as a Prompting Paradigm, 2025), and that metaphors in training data can causally drive cross-domain misalignment via latent features (Metaphors are a Source of Cross-Domain Misalignment, 2026). Grounding-theory work (Meaning without Reference, 2022; The Vector Grounding Problem, 2023; Mechanistic Emergence of Symbol Grounding, 2025) and abstract-concept work (BACH-V, 2026; How Deep is Love, 2025) study whether abstractions connect to concrete/perceptual representations, and BACH-V shows abstract value probes transfer to concrete events. However, NONE test the core CMT claim as a mechanism for reasoning: that abstract inference is *computed by importing structure from a concrete source domain*, that reasoning accuracy is a function of source-target STRUCTURAL ALIGNMENT (helping when isomorphic, harming when mismatched), or that this scaffold is a locatable, causally-steerable internal representation dissociable from surface metaphor phrasing. We uniquely turn CMT into a controlled structure-alignment law with a Location + Causal Intervention mechanism account, and add a high-stakes failure mode (mismatched metaphors corrupting inference).
Abstract: Conceptual Metaphor Theory holds that humans reason about abstract domains (time, quantity, social status, causation) by mapping them onto concrete source domains (space, physical size, verticality, force). We ask whether large language models do the same computationally: when an LLM reasons about an abstract target, does it recruit an internal representation of a concrete source domain and import that source's relational structure into its inference? We make three claims. First, structure-alignment law: for abstract reasoning problems whose correct answers depend on a specific relational structure, framing the problem with a metaphor whose source domain is structurally isomorphic to the target improves accuracy, whereas a structurally mismatched source (identical surface metaphor style, but wrong mapping) degrades it below a literal, metaphor-free baseline. This predicts a dose-response between source-target structural alignment and reasoning accuracy, and a diagnostic failure mode where a mismatched metaphor induces systematic, predictable errors. Second, representational recruitment: on abstract-reasoning trials, a probe trained only on concrete source-domain stimuli can decode the source-domain quantity from the model's hidden states, and this decodable source signal is stronger when the metaphor is aligned. Third, causal scaffold: the source-domain representation is a locatable direction that, when steered, changes abstract-reasoning behavior in the predicted direction and can rescue mismatched-metaphor errors or induce them under literal framing. Across several open-weight models we quantify the alignment law, the recruited-source-signal-to-behavior link, and steering controllability, reframing metaphor from decorative phrasing into a causal computational scaffold for machine abstraction.
Experiments: (1) Domain pairs and structure-controlled items: choose 4 abstract target domains with well-defined relational structure and canonical concrete source domains from CMT: (a) TIME<-SPACE (temporal ordering/duration comparisons), (b) QUANTITY<-VERTICALITY/SIZE (more-is-up, comparing amounts), (c) SOCIAL STATUS<-VERTICALITY (rank comparisons), (d) CAUSATION<-FORCE (which factor dominates an outcome). For each target build ~250 reasoning items (comparison, ordering, transitive-inference, and dominance problems) whose correct answer depends only on the underlying relational structure, with a labeled correct answer AND a labeled mismatch-lure (the answer that follows if a wrongly-oriented mapping is applied). (2) Framing conditions (within-item, content-matched, length-matched, format-enforced): (i) LITERAL baseline (no metaphor, plain relational statement); (ii) ALIGNED metaphor (frame via the canonical source with a correct-orientation mapping, e.g. 'later events are further ahead on the road'); (iii) MISMATCHED metaphor (same surface metaphor register but a structurally wrong mapping, e.g. reversed orientation or a source whose ordering contradicts the target); (iv) NEUTRAL-metaphor control (a metaphor from an irrelevant source with no structural bearing) to separate 'any figurative phrasing' from structure-specific effects. Validate alignment/mismatch labels with independent annotators. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (3) Behavioral structure-alignment law (mixed-effects: accuracy ~ framing * target_domain + (1|model|item)): predict ALIGNED > LITERAL > NEUTRAL ~ MISMATCHED, with MISMATCHED significantly BELOW literal and its errors concentrated on the mismatch-lure (the diagnostic signature that the model actually applied the wrong source structure rather than just getting confused). Add a graded-alignment variant (partially-consistent mappings) to test dose-response between a continuous source-target structural-alignment score and accuracy. (4) Location - recruited source signal: on abstract-reasoning trials, extract mid-layer hidden states; train a linear probe SOLELY on separate concrete source-domain stimuli (e.g. literal spatial/size/force comparisons) to decode the source-domain quantity, then test whether it decodes the corresponding quantity on the abstract trials (report per-layer AUROC/regression, held-out validated). Key test: source-quantity is decodable on abstract trials above a literal-only-probe baseline, and decodability is HIGHER under aligned than literal framing and MISORIENTED under mismatched framing (the probe reads the wrong value, predicting the behavioral lure). Correlate per-item recruited-source-signal strength/orientation with per-item accuracy and lure errors (Spearman). (5) Causal Intervention - scaffold steering: derive a source-domain direction via difference-in-means between high/low source-quantity concrete stimuli; (a) steer +correct-orientation during MISMATCHED or LITERAL framing and test whether it rescues/boosts abstract accuracy; (b) steer the wrong-orientation direction during LITERAL framing and test whether it induces the mismatch-lure errors (reproducing the metaphor's corrupting effect without any metaphor in the prompt). Compare against random-direction and no-steer controls; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (off-target reasoning and fluency preserved). (6) High-stakes transfer: replicate the CAUSATION<-FORCE mismatch condition on causal-attribution items in a consequential framing (e.g. medical/policy 'which factor drove the outcome' vignettes) to show a small, innocuous change in source-domain framing produces disproportionate, systematic causal-reasoning errors. (7) Metrics throughout: accuracy, mismatch-lure error rate, framing/interaction effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, structural-alignment dose-response slope, source-probe AUROC and orientation, recruited-signal-to-behavior correlation, and steering controllability (fraction of mismatch effect induced/rescued). Robustness: verify framing compliance, length matching, and that effects are not driven by per-language/per-domain difficulty.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Aligned vs mismatched framings may differ in fluency/plausibility rather than pure structure; mitigated by length/register matching, the neutral-metaphor control, annotator-validated alignment labels, and the content-matched steering that isolates the source representation from surface phrasing. (2) Instruction-tuned models may reason robustly from the literal content and ignore the metaphor, muting effects; a small/null alignment effect on aligned items would still be informative, and the MISMATCH-corruption prediction (metaphor actively hurting) is the sharpest, most novel test even if aligned metaphors merely match the literal baseline. (3) A probe trained on concrete stimuli decoding on abstract trials could reflect generic magnitude features shared by both rather than genuine source recruitment; mitigated by domain-specific probes, the orientation prediction under mismatch (probe reads the WRONG value in a way that predicts behavior), and random-direction steering controls. (4) The steering direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by orientation-specific (not just magnitude) predictions, specificity checks, and dose-response. (5) Some abstract domains may lack a single canonical source, making mismatch design ambiguous; we restrict to well-established CMT mappings and report robustness across the four pairs. (6) Effects may be model- or domain-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) The CMT framing is operationalized behaviorally/mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like embodied cognition.

Name: naming_as_compositional_chunking
Title: A Rose by a Shorter Name: Does Giving a Sub-Skill a Compact Label Let LLMs Compose It Into Novel Combinations?
Short Hypothesis: A central claim for why language powers intelligence is that it compresses reusable knowledge into compact, nameable chunks that can be recombined combinatorially. We hypothesize this operates inside LLMs at inference time: teaching a model a reusable sub-procedure under a compact NAME (a short lexical handle) lets it compose that sub-procedure into novel, unseen combinations more reliably than teaching the identical procedure spelled out verbosely each time, and the compact name creates a locatable, reusable internal 'subroutine' representation that is causally invoked during composition.
Related Work: A cluster of theory argues language aids intelligence by offering compact, culturally-evolved abstractions that enable generalization (How important is language for human-like intelligence?, 2025; Language as a bootstrap for compositional visual reasoning, 2021; Thinking in Words, 2014; Emergent Symbolic Cognition, 2025). Latent/implicit-reasoning work (Coconut, 2024; Implicit CoT via Distillation, 2023; Stepwise Internalization, 2024; A Survey on Latent Reasoning, 2025) shows reasoning can move out of verbal space entirely, and 'Why think step by step?' (2023) explains when intermediate steps help. Abstraction-of-Thought (2024) shows explicit abstraction layers improve reasoning. My own prior proposals covered iconic (sound-symbolic) naming aiding referent binding and lexicalization-gap effects on concept resolution. NONE of these isolate the *compression-for-composition* claim: that a compact name (versus a length-matched verbose description of the identical procedure) is what enables recombination into novel compositions, that this yields a compositional-generalization gain distinct from mere memorization or length, or that naming installs a reusable, causally-invokable internal subroutine. We uniquely turn the 'language compresses abstractions into reusable chunks' thesis into a controlled naming-vs-verbose intervention with a Location + Causal Intervention mechanism account, and tie it to a high-stakes agentic skill-composition setting.
Abstract: Why does language make minds more powerful? A leading answer is that language compresses reusable knowledge into compact, nameable chunks that can be freely recombined, turning a finite vocabulary into a combinatorial engine for novel thought. We test whether this compression-for-composition principle operates inside large language models. In-context, we teach a model a reusable sub-procedure (e.g., a small transformation on strings, lists, or graph states) in one of two ways that convey identical content: under a compact NAME (a short coined handle, 'let ZORP mean <procedure>') versus a length- and content-matched VERBOSE description that must be restated at each use. We then require the model to solve novel COMPOSITIONS — problems whose solutions chain the taught sub-procedure with others in combinations never demonstrated. Our central prediction is a naming-by-composition-depth interaction: compact naming yields a growing advantage on deeper/novel compositions, while offering little benefit on single-step reuse, and this advantage is not explained by prompt length, memorability, or surface repetition. We further predict compact naming reduces 'leakage' errors where the sub-procedure's internals bleed into unrelated steps. Mechanistically, we test whether a compact name installs a reusable subroutine: we probe for a 'named-primitive' representation activated whenever the name is invoked, measure whether it is reused with stable geometry across distinct compositions, and causally patch/steer it to trigger or suppress the sub-procedure's execution in novel contexts. Across several open-weight models we quantify the naming compositional-generalization gain, its dissociation from length and memorability, and mechanistic reuse, reframing 'naming' from labeling into a controllable lever for compositional intelligence.
Experiments: (1) Composable sub-skill suite with controllable depth: build synthetic domains where atomic sub-procedures can be freely chained and their compositions verified programmatically: (a) string transforms (e.g., a defined reversible substitution + rotation + filter), (b) list/state operations (map/filter/fold-style micro-ops with defined semantics), (c) small graph/gridworld state updates. For each domain define ~6 atomic sub-procedures; each has a compact coined NAME and a content-matched VERBOSE spelled-out description. Generate problems requiring compositions of depth 1-5, holding out ALL multi-step compositions from the teaching examples (novel-composition generalization). ~300 problems per depth, auto-graded. (2) Teaching conditions (in-context, content held constant): (i) NAMED - define each sub-procedure once with its compact name, then pose problems referring to procedures by name; (ii) VERBOSE - inline the full description at every use (length grows with reuse), matched in total demonstrated content; (iii) VERBOSE-once - define verbosely once then refer back by a long descriptive phrase (isolates 'compactness of the handle' from 'define-once'); (iv) ARBITRARY-LABEL control - a random unrelated label of equal length (rules out that any short token helps). Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (3) Core behavioral test (mixed-effects: accuracy ~ condition * composition_depth + (1|model|item)): predict NAMED >= VERBOSE-once > VERBOSE at depth 1 (small), with a WIDENING NAMED advantage as depth grows (naming x depth interaction), and ARBITRARY-LABEL below NAMED (compactness must be meaning-bearing, not just short). Report accuracy vs depth curves and the interaction coefficient with bootstrap CIs. (4) Confound controls: length-match total prompt tokens across NAMED and VERBOSE-once at each depth; add a memorability check (recall the sub-procedure's definition alone, without composition) to show any NAMED gain is compositional, not mere recall; vary name length/frequency to test that the effect tracks handle compactness. (5) Leakage/interference analysis: measure 'internals-leakage' errors where sub-procedure sub-steps intrude into unrelated composition steps; predict compact naming reduces leakage (a chunking signature), especially at high depth. (6) Location - named-primitive representation: on NAMED trials, extract hidden states at name-invocation tokens; train a linear probe to decode WHICH sub-procedure is being invoked (per-layer AUROC, held-out validated) and test whether the representation for a given name has stable geometry (high cosine similarity) across the different compositions it appears in (reuse signature), and whether it aligns with the representation induced by the VERBOSE description (naming compresses to the same primitive). (7) Causal Intervention - subroutine invocation: (a) Patching: cache the name-invocation activation from a NAMED context and patch it into a novel context lacking the name; test whether the sub-procedure's execution appears (sufficiency for triggering the subroutine). (b) Steering: derive a difference-in-means 'invoke-primitive' direction (name-present vs name-absent) and steer +direction to induce the sub-procedure and -direction to suppress it during composition; measure accuracy/leakage changes vs random-direction and no-steer controls; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (off-target sub-procedures and fluency preserved). (8) Mediation link: test whether per-item compositional-generalization gain correlates with named-primitive probe strength / reuse stability (Spearman). (9) High-stakes transfer: replicate in a simple agentic tool-composition setting where taught skills are API-like tools given compact names vs verbose call templates, and novel tasks require chaining tools in unseen combinations; measure task success vs composition depth. Metrics throughout: accuracy vs depth, naming x depth interaction, leakage-error rate, memorability control, probe AUROC and reuse-geometry stability, patching sufficiency rate, steering effect sizes, and mediation correlations, all with bootstrap CIs across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Compact names may help simply by shortening context and easing attention over long spans rather than via genuine chunking; mitigated by length-matching NAMED vs VERBOSE-once at each depth and by the ARBITRARY-LABEL control that isolates meaning-bearing compactness. (2) Tokenization may split coined names unpredictably, weakening the 'handle' signal; we test multiple name forms and models and report robustness. (3) Instruction-tuned models may already generalize compositions well, producing ceiling effects that hide differences; we increase composition depth, add distractor sub-procedures, and calibrate difficulty to mid-range. (4) A NAMED gain could reflect training-data familiarity with variable-binding syntax ('let X = ...') rather than compression per se; the VERBOSE-once condition (same define-once syntax, only handle length differs) isolates compactness. (5) The named-primitive direction may entangle with generic 'a definition was given' rather than a specific reusable subroutine; mitigated by which-procedure probes, reuse-geometry tests across compositions, random-direction steering, and specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (compact naming gives no compositional advantage over content-matched verbose descriptions) is itself highly informative: it would suggest LLM compositional generalization is content-driven rather than compression-driven, dissociating LLMs from the human 'language-as-chunking' account. (8) The chunking/compression framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim about human-like cognition.

Name: verbal_overshadowing_llm
Title: Words That Blur: Does Describing an Input in Language Corrupt an LLM's Own Fine-Grained Representation?
Short Hypothesis: Like humans, an LLM suffers verbal overshadowing: forcing it to verbally describe a rich, hard-to-verbalize stimulus before a fine-grained recognition/discrimination judgment degrades performance relative to no-description (and non-verbal-filler) baselines; crucially this is caused by the act of verbalization coarsening the model's internal representation of the item (recoding interference), it is strongest in modalities/domains the model lexicalizes poorly, and the degraded representation is locatable and causally recoverable.
Related Work: Verbal overshadowing (VO) is a robust human finding: verbally describing a face, taste, or object impairs subsequent non-verbal recognition (Schooler & Engstler-Schooler 1990; Meissner & Brigham 1997; the 1997/2001/2011 studies here), with computational models attributing it to recoding interference in which verbalization strips fine-grained detail from the maintained representation (Hatano et al. 2013/2015). Recent work shows VO is *stronger* in lexically-impoverished modalities such as taste (Zhuang & Vanek 2026), directly linking the effect to poverty of vocabulary. In LLMs/VLMs, prior interpretability work studies language bias in vision (Language-biased image classification 2022; When are Lemons Purple 2023), the binding problem (2024), and whether describing rather than seeing recovers performance (Analyzing Roles of Language and Vision 2024) — but ALL of these ask whether language *helps* or *biases* perception, and none test whether the *act of self-generated verbalization causally corrupts* a model's own maintained representation ahead of a fine-grained judgment. My prior proposals covered verbal interference via concurrent load, lexical gaps, and iconicity, but none test VO's core recoding-interference claim: that describing an item degrades the internal representation of *that item*. We are the first to (1) transfer VO into LLMs as a controlled describe-then-discriminate paradigm, (2) predict the lexical-impoverishment gradient (worst where the model has few words) and a high-stakes medical instance, and (3) give a Location + Causal Intervention account showing verbalization coarsens a recoverable internal fine-grained-detail representation.
Abstract: Humans who describe a face, a wine, or a suspect in words afterward recognize it worse than if they had stayed silent — verbal overshadowing — because putting a rich stimulus into language strips fine-grained, hard-to-verbalize detail from the memory that guides the later judgment. We ask whether large language models suffer the same self-inflicted damage: does forcing a model to describe an input in words before a fine-grained discrimination corrupt its own representation of that input? We construct describe-then-discriminate tasks where a target item (a detailed textual scene/object description, a numeric/structured pattern, a code snippet, or a clinical vignette) is presented, then the model must either (a) verbalize the item in free-form words or (b) perform a non-verbal filler / stay silent, and finally answer a fine-grained recognition or discrimination question separating the target from a near-neighbor distractor. We predict a verbal-overshadowing effect: self-generated description lowers fine-grained accuracy relative to no-description and filler controls, is selective to items requiring fine-grained (not gist) discrimination, and — mirroring the human taste finding — is largest in domains the model lexicalizes poorly, where description forces lossy compression. Mechanistically, we test the recoding-interference account: a probe decoding fine-grained target detail from hidden states should show reduced decodability after verbalization, this representational blurring should predict the behavioral drop item-by-item, and steering along or restoring a fine-grained-detail direction should cancel the overshadowing. Across several open-weight models we quantify the VO effect, its lexical-poverty gradient, a high-stakes clinical instance, and its mechanistic mediation, reframing verbalization from a neutral readout into an act that can actively degrade machine representation.
Experiments: (1) Describe-then-discriminate battery: build ~250 items per domain across four domains spanning a lexicalization gradient: (a) richly-lexicalized textual scenes/objects, (b) structured numeric/visual-pattern descriptions (poorly lexicalized), (c) code snippets, (d) clinical vignettes (high-stakes). Each item has a target and a near-neighbor DISTRACTOR differing in a fine-grained detail, plus a matched GIST-level control question answerable from coarse features (selectivity control). Ground truth is known and auto-checkable. (2) Interference conditions (content held constant): (i) NO-DESCRIPTION baseline — target shown, then immediately the discrimination question; (ii) VERBALIZE — after the target, the model must produce a free-form verbal description of it before the question (recoding manipulation); (iii) NON-VERBAL FILLER — an equal-length unrelated numeric/tally task between target and question (controls for delay/context length without verbalization); (iv) COPY control — reproduce the target verbatim (controls for re-processing without lossy re-description). Enforce format; verify compliance. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (3) Core behavioral test (mixed-effects: accuracy ~ condition * question_grain + (1|model|item)): predict VERBALIZE lowers FINE-GRAINED accuracy below NO-DESCRIPTION, FILLER, and COPY (isolating verbalization, not delay/reprocessing), with little/no effect on GIST questions (condition x grain interaction) — the signature that describing selectively destroys fine detail. (4) Lexical-poverty gradient: predict the VO effect size is largest in poorly-lexicalized domains (numeric patterns, subtle clinical findings) and smallest in richly-lexicalized scenes, mirroring the human taste result; quantify per-domain lexicalization with a description-compressibility proxy (description length / distinctiveness) and correlate it with per-domain VO magnitude. (5) High-stakes clinical instance: in the clinical-vignette domain, test whether forcing the model to first verbalize a differential-description of a case before choosing between two similar diagnoses raises diagnostic error on fine-distinction cases relative to answering directly — a small, innocuous 'describe your reasoning first' prompt causing disproportionate fine-grained error. (6) Location — fine-grained-detail probe: extract hidden states at the pre-answer position; train a probe to decode the target's fine-grained distinguishing feature (per-layer AUROC, held-out validated) under each condition; predict lower decodability after VERBALIZE than NO-DESCRIPTION/COPY (representational blurring). (7) Mediation: test whether per-item drop in probe decodability predicts per-item accuracy drop under verbalization (Spearman). (8) Causal Intervention: (a) cache the pre-verbalization fine-detail representation and patch it back in after verbalization — predict it rescues fine-grained accuracy (recoding interference is recoverable, detail was degraded not deleted); (b) derive a difference-in-means 'fine-detail' direction (high vs low distinguishing-feature contrast) and steer +direction after verbalization to test recovery, and -direction under NO-DESCRIPTION to test induction of overshadowing without any description; compare to random-direction and no-steer controls; report sign, dose-response, specificity (gist accuracy and fluency preserved). Metrics throughout: fine/gist accuracy, condition x grain interaction effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, VO magnitude per domain and its correlation with lexicalization, probe AUROC drop, blurring-to-behavior correlation, patching rescue rate, and steering effect sizes across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Verbalization adds tokens/delay that could impair via context length rather than recoding; mitigated by the length-matched non-verbal FILLER and verbatim-COPY controls and by testing the fine-vs-gist INTERACTION rather than raw drops. (2) Instruction-tuned models may re-access the original target tokens (still in context) and avoid overshadowing entirely, unlike humans who lose sensory access; we test both keeping and removing the target from context (a memory-maintenance variant that better matches the human paradigm) and report both — a null in the target-present variant with an effect in the target-removed variant would still cleanly confirm recoding interference. (3) The fine-detail probe may capture surface tokens rather than a maintained representation; mitigated by target-removed trials, held-out validation, matched positions, and random-direction steering controls. (4) VO effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models, domains, and report effect sizes with CIs. (5) A null result (verbalization does not degrade fine-grained judgment) is itself highly informative: it would dissociate LLMs from the human recoding-interference account, suggesting verbalization in LLMs is a lossless readout rather than a lossy recoding. (6) The verbal-overshadowing framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like memory.

Name: exact_number_word_gating
Title: One, Two, Many: Does the Availability of an Exact Number Word Gate Whether an LLM Holds an Exact vs. Approximate Quantity?
Short Hypothesis: The strong-Whorfian anumeric-language finding transfers into LLMs at inference time: an LLM's ability to store and operate on an EXACT quantity is gated by whether a compact exact number WORD is available in the representation it is using; when the exact word is unavailable (an 'anumeric' regime induced by forcing approximate quantifiers, a low-numeracy pivot language, or ablating a number-word feature), the model silently falls back to an approximate, magnitude-based (log/Weber-law) representation, producing exactly the ratio-dependent error signature of anumeric human speakers rather than random noise.
Related Work: Human cross-cultural work shows exact number cognition depends on number WORDS: anumeric Amazonian speakers fail exact-matching beyond ~3 while their approximate number sense is intact (Frank/Everett/Gibson 2008; da Silva Sinha et al. 2026), and verbal interference selectively suppresses EXACT (not approximate) numerical representation in numerate adults (Frank, Fedorenko, Lai, Saxe, Gibson 2011). Number-word procedures, not perception, are argued to be the origin of exact integers (Schneider/Barner 2017; Cross-cultural routines, Everett 2012). In LLMs, a rich interpretability literature characterizes number REPRESENTATIONS (sublinear/log mental-number-line, Number Representations 2025; sinusoidal precise encoding, Pre-trained LMs Learn Accurate Number Representations 2025; stable relational geometry, The Representational Geometry of Number 2026) and COUNTING mechanisms (internal-counter heads, CountScope 2025; System-2 counting 2026; Sequential Enumeration 2025). CRUCIALLY, all LLM work studies how numbers are encoded/counted assuming the number word exists; NONE test the strong-Whorfian gating claim — that removing the exact number word (via approximate-quantifier framing, a low-numeracy pivot language, or ablating a number-word feature) causally forces a fallback from exact to approximate magnitude cognition, reproducing the ratio-dependent anumeric error signature. My prior proposals covered lexical gaps, tokenization granularity, and verbal interference via concurrent load, but none isolate exact-number-word availability as the switch between exact and approximate quantity behavior. We uniquely transfer the anumeric finding as a controlled availability manipulation with a Location + Causal Intervention mechanistic account and a high-stakes medical-dosing instance.
Abstract: One of the strongest claims about language and thought is that exact number cognition depends on possessing exact number words: speakers of 'anumeric' languages, and numerate adults under verbal interference, can approximate quantities but cannot reliably represent exact ones beyond three, while their approximate number sense stays intact. We ask whether the same dependence governs large language models. We hypothesize that an LLM's capacity to store and manipulate an EXACT quantity is gated by whether a compact exact number word is available in the representation it is currently using; when that word is unavailable, the model silently reverts to an approximate, magnitude-based representation and produces the ratio-dependent (Weber-law) error signature characteristic of anumeric humans rather than random errors. We induce three 'anumeric' regimes on identical exact-quantity problems: (i) approximate-quantifier framing that forbids exact numerals ('several', 'many'), (ii) prompting in a low-numeracy pivot language, and (iii) ablating a located number-word feature. Across exact matching, exact subtraction, and set-equality tasks we test whether these regimes selectively degrade EXACT performance while sparing APPROXIMATE (larger-vs-smaller) judgments, and whether the residual errors follow a distance/ratio-dependent curve, the hallmark of a magnitude fallback. Mechanistically, we locate an exact-number-word representation, show it is decodable on success and degraded under anumeric regimes, and causally steer it to induce or rescue the exact-to-approximate fallback. We include a high-stakes medical-dosing instance where approximate framing silently converts exact doses into ratio-dependent errors. Across several open-weight models we quantify the gating effect, its exact-vs-approximate selectivity, the anumeric error signature, and mechanistic mediation, delivering the first mechanistic test of whether exact number words gate machine exact-number cognition.
Experiments: (1) Quantity-task battery separating EXACT from APPROXIMATE demand: build ~300 items each for (a) exact matching (produce/verify a set of exactly N items, N up to ~20), (b) exact subtraction/addition on set sizes, (c) set-equality ('are these two sets exactly equal?'), each paired with a matched APPROXIMATE control question over the identical stimulus ('which set is larger?', 'roughly how many?') that requires only magnitude, not exact value. Ground truth known and auto-checkable; items span a range of target values and, for equality/comparison, a range of ratios between the two sets (to fit a Weber-law error curve). (2) Anumeric-regime manipulations (content held constant): (i) NUMERATE baseline (exact numerals allowed); (ii) APPROXIMATE-QUANTIFIER framing that forbids exact numerals and forces vague quantifiers ('a few', 'several', 'many') for intermediate representations while still requiring an exact final answer; (iii) LOW-NUMERACY PIVOT LANGUAGE (present/require reasoning in a language with restricted or unusual numeral systems relative to the model's strong languages, back-translation checked); (iv) VERBAL-INTERFERENCE control adapting the human paradigm (interleave a demanding same-domain verbal task). Enforce format; verify compliance. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B. (3) Core behavioral test (mixed-effects: accuracy ~ regime * task_type + (1|model|item)): predict anumeric regimes selectively degrade EXACT tasks (matching, exact subtraction, equality) while sparing APPROXIMATE comparison (regime x task_type interaction) — the signature that the word, not the magnitude, is what is lost. (4) Anumeric error-signature test: on the degraded exact trials, test whether errors are ratio/distance-dependent (probability of error rises as the two quantities' ratio approaches 1, and error magnitude scales with target value per Weber's law) rather than uniform/random; fit a Weber fraction per regime and compare to the numerate baseline. A ratio-dependent curve is the diagnostic of a magnitude fallback. (5) Small-number floor: test whether exact performance survives for very small N (~1-3) even under anumeric regimes (the human 'subitizing'/small-number-word floor), predicting a subitizing-like plateau. (6) High-stakes medical instance: replicate the APPROXIMATE-QUANTIFIER regime on clinical dosing/count vignettes (e.g., 'administer several units', pill/dose counting) and test whether approximate framing silently converts exact-dose decisions into ratio-dependent errors — a small innocuous framing change causing disproportionate exact-quantity failure. (7) Location — exact-number-word representation: contrast hidden states on exact-success vs exact-failure trials and on numerate-vs-anumeric framings; train a linear probe to decode the exact value and, separately, whether an exact-number-word is 'active' (per-layer AUROC, held-out validated); predict lower exact-value decodability and weaker word-active signal under anumeric regimes. (8) Mediation: test whether per-item drop in exact-word/exact-value decodability predicts per-item exact-accuracy drop (Spearman).
