(9) A null result (self-translation preserves meaning) is itself informative, showing LLM cross-lingual re-expression is lossless unlike the human self-translation cost. (10) The self-translation framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like bilingual cognition.

Name: translation_crutch_grammar_induction
Title: Grammar Book or Bilingual Dictionary? Testing Whether LLMs Learn a Novel Language In-Context by Building a Grammar or Leaning on a Translation Crutch
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is given a novel language in-context (a mini grammar plus examples), it does not induce a genuine standalone grammar; instead it leans on a 'translation crutch,' covertly mapping each construction back to a pivot language and generating via that pivot. The strength of this crutch grows with typological distance from the model's training languages, causally bounds how well the model generalizes to unseen constructions, and is a locatable, steerable internal signal: suppressing the crutch forces (and, for near-typology languages, improves) genuine grammar use, while amplifying it induces pivot-shaped errors.
Related Work: Recent work shows LLMs can do some explicit in-context language learning from grammar-book explanations ('Explicit Learning and the LLM in MT', 2025) and that learnability degrades with typological implausibility both in pretraining ('Can LMs Learn Typologically Implausible Languages?', 2025) and constructed-language studies (Culbertson & Kirby 2011). In-context language learning has been mechanistically tied to n-gram/induction heads ('In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms', 2024), and multilingual work shows shared cross-lingual syntactic circuits with a language-independent pivot direction ('The Same But Different', 2024; 'On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages', 2024) and English-shaped pivot routing. All of this either (a) measures behavioral learnability without asking HOW the model represents the novel language, or (b) studies pivot routing only for KNOWN languages present in training. None ask whether in-context learning of a genuinely novel language is a real grammar induction or a covert translation-to-pivot process, whether that crutch scales with typological distance, whether it causally caps generalization to unseen constructions, or whether it is a locatable/steerable component. We uniquely reframe in-context language learning as a translation-crutch-vs-native-grammar dissociation with a Location + Causal Intervention account.
Abstract: Give a large language model a short grammar and a handful of examples of a language it has never seen, and it will often produce plausible new sentences. But is it inducing a genuine grammar, or is it quietly translating every construction back to a language it already knows and generating through that crutch? We propose the translation-crutch hypothesis: in-context learning of a novel language proceeds largely by covert mapping to a pivot (typically English-shaped) representation rather than by building a standalone grammar, that reliance on this crutch grows with the novel language's typological distance from the model's training languages, and that the crutch causally limits generalization to constructions not derivable by pivot-style word-for-word mapping (e.g., non-canonical word order, agreement, and morphology absent from the pivot). We construct controlled artificial languages that systematically vary typological distance from English (word order, case marking, agreement, morphological richness), each presented in-context via a mini grammar plus examples, and test generalization to held-out construction types. Behaviorally, we predict a distance-graded generalization cliff concentrated on pivot-incompatible constructions, with characteristic pivot-shaped errors (e.g., defaulting to English word order or dropping agreement). Mechanistically, we locate a 'pivot-translation' representation via probing (can the pivot-language gloss be decoded from hidden states during novel-language generation?) and test causally: suppressing this component should force genuine grammar use and improve near-typology generalization while hurting far-typology output, and amplifying it should induce pivot-shaped errors. Across several open-weight models we quantify the crutch, its typological-distance scaling, its causal cap on generalization, and steering controllability, reframing in-context language learning as translation rather than acquisition.
Experiments: (1) Controlled artificial-language suite: build ~6-8 synthetic languages that share a fixed lexicon (nonce content words plus a small function-word inventory) but vary along typological axes graded by distance from English: (a) word order (SVO baseline -> SOV -> VSO -> free order with case), (b) overt case marking (none -> nominative/accusative suffixes), (c) subject-verb and adjective-noun agreement (none -> gender/number agreement), (d) morphological richness (isolating -> agglutinative suffix stacking). Each language comes with a compact in-context 'grammar book' (rules stated in English) plus ~15-30 example sentence pairs (novel-language <-> English gloss). Define a per-language typological-distance score from the number/type of features diverging from English. (2) Generalization test with held-out constructions: for each language, hold out entire construction TYPES from the in-context examples (e.g., show only declaratives, test questions; show only singular agreement, test plural; show only intransitives, test ditransitives). Measure production/comprehension accuracy on held-out constructions via translation-into and translation-out-of the novel language and grammaticality judgments over minimal pairs. Auto-grade against the ground-truth generative grammar. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B. (3) Behavioral distance-graded cliff (mixed-effects: accuracy ~ typological_distance * construction_pivot_compatibility + (1|model|item)): predict accuracy on PIVOT-INCOMPATIBLE held-out constructions (non-English word order, agreement, morphology) falls steeply with typological distance, while pivot-compatible constructions stay high; characterize the error signature (fraction of errors that are pivot-shaped, e.g., English-default word order, dropped agreement suffixes) as the diagnostic that the model translated rather than acquired. (4) Location - pivot-translation representation: during novel-language generation, extract hidden states at content and function-word positions; train a linear probe to decode (i) the corresponding English gloss token and (ii) whether the model is in a 'pivot-translating' vs 'native-generating' state, using contrasts between near-typology (English-like) and far-typology sentences (per-layer AUROC, held-out validated). Predict pivot-gloss decodability is high and RISES with typological distance and on error trials. (5) Mediation: test whether per-item pivot-gloss decodability predicts per-item generalization error on pivot-incompatible constructions (Spearman), linking the crutch to the behavioral cliff. (6) Causal Intervention: derive a difference-in-means 'pivot-translation' direction (pivot-translating vs native-generating contrasts); (a) SUPPRESS by subtracting the direction during generation and test whether it reduces pivot-shaped errors and improves agreement/word-order compliance on near-typology languages (and whether it hurts far-typology output where the crutch is the only route), (b) AMPLIFY to induce pivot-shaped errors (English word order / dropped morphology) even on well-learned constructions; compare against random-direction and no-steer controls; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (lexical accuracy and fluency preserved). (7) Grammar-book vs examples ablation: vary whether the in-context material is rule-based (explicit grammar) vs example-only, testing whether explicit rules reduce crutch reliance or merely improve pivot-compatible constructions. (8) Robustness: vary the number of in-context examples, lexicon overlap, and (for a model with a non-English pivot) test whether the crutch tracks THAT pivot's typology rather than English, directly tying the effect to the model's dominant language. Metrics throughout: held-out construction accuracy, pivot-shaped error rate, distance x pivot-compatibility interaction effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, pivot-gloss probe AUROC and its scaling with distance, mediation correlations, and steering suppress/amplify effect sizes across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Artificial languages may be too easy or too hard, flattening the distance-graded cliff; we calibrate feature counts and example numbers to mid-range difficulty and report the full distance sweep. (2) A pivot-gloss probe decoding English during generation could reflect the in-context English glosses still present in context rather than a genuine internal translation step; we mitigate by removing glosses from context at test time, probing at matched positions, and using near-vs-far typology contrasts and the causal steering test (which manipulates the representation, not the prompt). (3) Suppressing the crutch may broadly degrade generation, confounding the near-typology improvement claim; we use random-direction and matched-magnitude controls and test the predicted DISSOCIATION (helps near-typology, hurts far-typology) rather than a uniform effect. (4) 'Typological distance from training languages' is approximate and model-specific; the non-English-pivot crossover test and per-model distance scoring address this. (5) Instruction-tuned models may already do robust in-context grammar induction, muting the crutch; we include base variants, harder morphology, and multiple models, and report effect sizes. (6) Auto-grading against a generative grammar may miss acceptable variation; we use minimal-pair grammaticality judgments and human spot-checks. (7) A null result (no translation crutch; generalization independent of typological distance and pivot-decodability) is itself highly informative: it would show LLMs perform genuine in-context grammar induction rather than covert translation, a strong positive claim about language-learning ability. (8) The 'crutch/acquisition' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim about human-like language acquisition.

Name: pragmatic_enrichment_default
Title: Reading Between the Lines When You Shouldn't: A Pragmatic-Enrichment Default as a Hidden Reasoning Failure Mode in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs, like humans, apply a pragmatic-enrichment default — spontaneously upgrading literal meaning with Gricean inferences (scalar implicature 'some'→'not all', exhaustivity, relevance-driven additions) — and this default is beneficial for cooperative dialogue but silently corrupts tasks that require the strict literal reading (formal logic, contracts, statutes, clinical instructions). This enrichment is a locatable, steerable internal 'pragmatic-mode' signal that fires by default; suppressing it at literal-mode tasks reduces enrichment errors, while amplifying it induces them even on cases where the literal reading is required.
Related Work: Existing LLM pragmatics work is behavioral or competence-oriented: LLMs partly detect implicatures and improve with Gricean CoT prompting (Is the Pope Catholic? 2023), fall short of humans on implicature/presupposition/speech acts (Pragmatic Competence Without Embodiment 2025; Manner Implicatures 2024; Are BabyLMs Deaf to Gricean Maxims 2025), and neural encoders predict scalar-inference strength from linguistic features (Harnessing the Linguistic Signal 2020). Ambiguity work locates sparse Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons that steer answering vs abstention (Sparse Neurons 2025), and loophole work shows models exploit scalar implicature (LLMs Identify Ambiguities and Exploit Loopholes 2025). ALL of this treats pragmatic enrichment as a capacity to be measured or improved. NONE frame enrichment as a DEFAULT that mis-fires as a reasoning FAILURE MODE on literal-required tasks, isolate a controllable literal-vs-enriched internal mode, test whether it causally CAUSES errors on formal/legal/clinical text, or provide a Location + Causal Intervention account with a suppression fix. My prior proposals covered ambiguity-branch collapse, evidentiality, counterfactual mood, and canonicalization but never pragmatic enrichment / the Quantity maxim as a default reasoning liability. We uniquely flip pragmatics from a desired competence into a diagnosable, steerable hazard.
Abstract: Cooperative communication depends on going beyond literal meaning: when a speaker says 'some students passed,' listeners infer 'not all.' Large language models reproduce these pragmatic enrichments, and prior work treats this as a competence to celebrate. We argue the opposite is also true: pragmatic enrichment is a DEFAULT that silently corrupts reasoning whenever the task actually requires the strict literal reading — formal logic, contracts, statutes, and clinical instructions, where 'some' must mean 'at least one', an unstated condition must not be assumed, and only what is written counts. We hypothesize that an LLM carries a controllable internal 'pragmatic-mode' signal governing whether it computes literal or enriched meaning, that this mode is engaged by default, and that it is a proximal cause of systematic errors on literal-required tasks. We make three claims. First, the enrichment default is real and harmful: on matched items differing only in whether the correct answer needs the literal or the enriched reading, models over-enrich, producing characteristic errors (treating 'some' as 'not all' in a valid syllogism, importing unstated exceptions into a contract clause). Second, mode is diagnostic: a probe reads literal-vs-enriched processing from hidden states and predicts these errors before they surface. Third, mode is causal and fixable: steering down a located pragmatic-enrichment direction reduces literal-task errors, while steering it up induces enrichment even where the literal reading is required. We evaluate across several open-weight models on logic, contract, and clinical-instruction tasks, plus a high-stakes medical instance where over-reading a literal dosing instruction is dangerous, quantifying the default, its mechanistic mediation, and steering controllability.
Experiments: (1) Literal-vs-enriched matched battery: build ~250 items per domain where the correct answer hinges on interpretation mode, each in matched pairs differing ONLY in whether the LITERAL or the ENRICHED reading is correct, with a labeled enrichment-error lure. Domains: (a) scalar implicature in logic — syllogisms/entailments where treating 'some' as 'not all' (or 'or' as exclusive) flips validity; (b) exhaustivity/presupposition in contracts — clauses where importing an unstated exception or reading a list as exhaustive changes the legal answer; (c) clinical instructions — directives where enriching a literal statement (e.g. inferring an implied 'as needed' or an unstated stop condition) changes the action. Include matched cooperative-dialogue controls where enrichment IS correct (selectivity). Ground truth auto-checkable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (2) Behavioral default test (mixed-effects: accuracy/enrichment-lure-rate ~ required_mode * domain + (1|model|item)): predict models over-enrich — higher error and enrichment-lure rate on LITERAL-required items than enriched-required items, with errors concentrated on the enrichment lure (the diagnostic that the model read in an unstated inference), while cooperative-dialogue controls stay accurate. Test whether explicit 'interpret literally' prompting only partially closes the gap (default persists). (3) Location — pragmatic-mode signal: contrast hidden states on literal-vs-enriched processing (matched-pair items, and enrichment-correct vs enrichment-error trials); train a linear probe to decode whether the model is in enriched vs literal mode (per-layer AUROC, held-out validated); derive a difference-in-means 'pragmatic-enrichment' direction. Predict enrichment-mode is engaged by default (high baseline projection) and higher on error trials. (4) Mediation: test whether per-item enrichment-mode projection predicts per-item literal-task error (Spearman) and mediates required_mode→error. (5) Causal Intervention: steer -enrichment-direction on literal-required items to test error REDUCTION (recovering literal reading), and +enrichment-direction to INDUCE enrichment errors even on literal-required items and on cooperative controls; compare against random-direction and no-steer controls; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (cooperative-dialogue accuracy and fluency preserved — crucially, suppression should NOT harm items where enrichment is correct). (6) High-stakes clinical instance: on dosing/instruction vignettes where the safe action requires the literal reading (do exactly what is written, do not infer unstated conditions), test whether the enrichment default produces unsafe over-reading and whether -enrichment steering reduces unsafe actions on fine-distinction cases. (7) Robustness: vary implicature type (scalar, exhaustivity, manner), test that the direction generalizes across domains, and check the default's dependence on model scale. Metrics throughout: accuracy, enrichment-lure rate, required_mode x domain interaction effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, enrichment-mode probe AUROC, mediation correlations, steering reduce/induce effect sizes, cooperative-control specificity, and clinical unsafe-action rate across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Errors on literal-required items could stem from general difficulty rather than genuine pragmatic enrichment; mitigated by matched literal/enriched pairs (same surface content), the enrichment-lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC enriched reading, not random), and the cooperative-dialogue selectivity control. (2) Instruction-tuned models may already read literally when in a formal register, muting the default; we include base variants, harder items, and test whether 'interpret literally' prompting only partially closes the gap. (3) The enrichment direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by matched literal/enriched contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and the crucial specificity test that suppression preserves cooperative-control accuracy (a generic push would hurt it). (4) Suppressing enrichment could globally flatten pragmatic ability; we explicitly measure and require preserved performance on enrichment-correct items, framing the goal as a controllable mode switch, not permanent removal. (5) Legal/clinical ground truth can be contestable; we use items with clear literal-correct answers and expert spot-checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (no enrichment default, or literal errors are not enrichment-shaped) is itself informative — it would show LLM pragmatic inference is contextually gated rather than a default liability. (8) The Gricean/pragmatics framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like communicative intent.

Name: doubt_marker_gating
Title: A Word for Doubt: Do Metacognitive Discourse Markers Causally Gate an LLM's Error Correction, or Are They Just Surface Style?
Short Hypothesis: The specific metacognitive discourse markers an LLM emits mid-reasoning ('wait', 'actually', 'but', 'hmm', 'however') are not interchangeable stylistic decorations: each marker's lexical identity causally recruits a distinct error-monitoring/revision computation, so that (a) forcing an appropriate doubt marker at a hidden error step triggers correction the model would otherwise skip, (b) marker identity carries graded information about whether and how the model will revise, and (c) suppressing the model's own emitted marker aborts an in-progress correction. In short, the model needs a word for doubt to enact doubt.
Related Work: Recent interpretability work extracts a single holistic 'reflection direction' and steers reflection frequency (ReflCtrl 2025; From Emergence to Control 2025), traces layer-wise reflection onset through discourse-cue competition (From Latent Signals to Reflection Behavior 2026), shows reflection correlates with internal uncertainty (ReflCtrl 2025), and that error-detection is decodable from activations (Probing for Arithmetic Errors 2025; The Validation Gap 2025). Self-correction studies (Dissociation of Faithful/Unfaithful Reasoning 2024; Understanding the Dark Side 2024; Accuracy-Correction Paradox 2025) show correction is brittle and sometimes causes answer-wavering. Crucially, ALL of this treats reflection as a single latent behavior/direction and treats the surface discourse markers as an epiphenomenal readout of an underlying decision. NONE ask whether the LEXICAL IDENTITY of the emitted marker is itself causally functional — whether different doubt words ('wait' vs 'actually' vs 'but') recruit different revision computations, whether inserting the RIGHT marker (vs a wrong or generic one) at a hidden error step gates correction, or whether the marker is a linguistic tool the model needs to enact revision rather than a byproduct of an already-made revision decision. This reframes the language<->intelligence question at the level of individual metacognitive words and distinguishes us from holistic reflection-vector and error-probe work.
Abstract: When people catch themselves making a mistake they often say 'wait' or 'actually' — self-directed words that mark and license a correction. Large language models sprinkle the same markers through their chains of thought, and prior interpretability work treats these markers as surface readouts of an underlying, holistic 'reflection' decision. We test the opposite, stronger claim: that the specific metacognitive discourse marker is a causally functional linguistic tool, and that the model needs the right word for doubt in order to enact doubt. We make three claims. First, marker identity is informative and distinct: different doubt markers ('wait', 'actually', 'but', 'however', 'hmm') precede systematically different revision outcomes (full backtrack vs local edit vs no change), and are carried by partly distinct internal signals rather than one reflection direction. Second, markers causally gate correction: at reasoning steps containing a hidden, latent error the model is about to propagate, forcing the appropriate doubt marker triggers correction the model would otherwise skip, while forcing a mismatched or a neutral filler marker does not — isolating lexical content from mere token insertion. Third, markers are necessary, not epiphenomenal: suppressing the model's own spontaneously emitted marker (via constrained decoding or activation intervention) aborts an in-progress correction, driving the model to propagate the error. We evaluate on math, logic, and multi-hop QA with injected latent errors across several open-weight reasoning models, and add a high-stakes clinical-reasoning instance where the absence of a doubt word lets a wrong provisional diagnosis stand. Our work reframes metacognitive markers from stylistic residue into causal, language-borne machinery for machine self-correction.
Experiments: (1) Marker taxonomy and revision-outcome mapping: from natural chains of thought on GSM8K/MATH, deductive logic chains (depth 2-6), and 2WikiMultiHop-style QA, segment traces into steps and detect metacognitive markers (wait, actually, but, however, hmm, let me reconsider, hold on). For each marker occurrence, label the downstream revision outcome (no change / local numeric-or-fact edit / full backtrack-and-restart) via automatic diff of the pre- and post-marker reasoning against ground truth. Test (multinomial mixed-effects: revision_type ~ marker_identity + step_difficulty + (1|model|item)) whether marker identity predicts revision type beyond position/difficulty. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B and its reasoning variant, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-distill-Qwen-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (2) Latent-error injection benchmark: on items the model solves correctly under free reasoning, inject a controlled error into a specified step (wrong intermediate value / invalid inference) and truncate the trace at the point just after the error, so continuation determines whether the model catches it. This yields matched 'hidden-error' steps where correction is warranted. (3) Causal marker-gating test (sufficiency): at the post-error continuation point, force the next tokens to be (i) an APPROPRIATE doubt marker ('wait,' / 'actually,'), (ii) a MISMATCHED marker (a connective implying agreement, 'therefore,' / 'so,'), (iii) a NEUTRAL FILLER of equal length ('okay,' / a nonce-but-fluent phrase), and (iv) FREE continuation (baseline). Measure correction rate (does the model fix the injected error and reach the right answer) per condition. Key prediction (mixed-effects: corrected ~ marker_condition + (1|model|item)): appropriate doubt markers raise correction over free/neutral/mismatched, isolating lexical content (the neutral-filler and mismatched controls rule out mere token insertion or 'more tokens'). Report sign, dose (single vs repeated marker), and specificity (on NO-error control items, forcing a doubt marker should not spuriously break correct reasoning). (4) Marker granularity: test whether specific markers selectively induce specific revision types (e.g., 'wait' -> full backtrack; 'actually' -> local edit) by measuring the revision-type distribution each forced marker produces on matched hidden-error steps. (5) Location: contrast hidden states at pre-marker positions on trials that will vs won't revise; train a linear probe to (a) predict whether a revision is impending and (b) decode which marker the model is about to emit (per-layer AUROC, held-out validated). Test whether distinct markers have partly separable directions (pairwise linear separability) rather than collapsing onto one reflection axis, and compare a marker-specific probe against a single-reflection-direction baseline for predicting correction. (6) Necessity test (suppression): on trials where the model SPONTANEOUSLY emits a doubt marker and then corrects, suppress that marker two ways — (a) constrained decoding that bans the marker tokens at that position, and (b) subtracting the located marker direction from the residual stream at that position — and measure whether correction is aborted (error propagated to final answer) relative to a random-token-ban and random-direction control. Prediction: suppressing the model's own doubt marker aborts correction, showing the marker is necessary, not a byproduct. (7) Mediation: test whether per-item marker-probe strength predicts per-item correction and whether forced-marker-induced correction gain is mediated by increased engagement of the marker direction (Spearman). (8) High-stakes clinical instance: on differential-diagnosis vignettes, inject a plausible-but-wrong provisional diagnosis mid-reasoning; test whether the absence of a doubt marker lets it stand (confident misdiagnosis) and whether forcing an appropriate doubt marker at that step rescues the correct diagnosis on fine-distinction cases, vs neutral-filler control. Metrics throughout: revision-type prediction accuracy, correction rate per marker condition with bootstrap CIs, marker-condition and necessity effect sizes, no-error specificity, probe AUROC and pairwise marker separability, mediation correlations, and clinical misdiagnosis rate across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Forcing a doubt marker may help simply by adding a pause/extra tokens rather than via lexical meaning; mitigated by the length-matched NEUTRAL FILLER and MISMATCHED-marker controls and by testing marker-specific revision-type selectivity (a generic 'more tokens' account predicts no marker-type differentiation). (2) Reasoning-tuned models may correct robustly regardless of marker, yielding ceiling effects; we use latent-error injection to create genuine hidden-error steps, include base/non-reasoning variants, and calibrate error difficulty. (3) Suppression via token-banning may push probability onto a synonymous marker, masking necessity; we ban the full doubt-marker synonym set and cross-check with the activation-subtraction suppression and random-token/random-direction controls. (4) Automatic labeling of revision type (backtrack vs local edit) is noisy; we use ground-truth-anchored diffs, multiple thresholds, and human spot-checks on a sample. (5) Marker directions may entangle with generic uncertainty rather than marker identity; mitigated by matched will-revise/won't-revise contrasts, pairwise-separability tests against a single-reflection-direction baseline, held-out probe validation, and specificity controls. (6) Effects may be model-specific; we test several models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result — markers are interchangeable surface style, forcing/suppressing them does not gate correction — is itself highly informative, showing LLM self-correction is decided pre-lexically and the discourse marker is a pure readout, cleanly dissociating the enactment of revision from the language that names it. (8) The 'word for doubt' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like metacognitive experience.

Name: affect_labeling_debiasing
Title: Name It to Tame It: Does an LLM's Own Affect-Labeling Decouple Its Reasoning From Emotional Content?
Short Hypothesis: The human 'affect labeling' effect — putting a feeling into a compact emotion word incidentally dampens its influence on judgment — transfers to LLMs: requiring a model to first name the emotional content of an affect-laden input causally reduces the emotion's distorting pull on its subsequent reasoning (fewer affect-driven errors, better calibration on affective content), and this debiasing is mediated by a locatable affect-representation whose engagement drops after labeling and can be causally steered.
Related Work: Human affect-labeling research shows that verbally labeling an emotion incidentally (without intentional reappraisal) reduces amygdala/limbic responses and self-reported distress, distinct from and cheaper than reappraisal (Torre & Lieberman meta-analysis; Burklund et al. 2014, 116 cites; Lieberman fMRI/ERP, third-person self-talk 2017, 111 cites; Brooks et al. neuroimaging meta-analysis 2016, 128 cites), and that labeling in a second language further increases emotional distance (Morawetz et al. 2017). In LLMs, prior work studies emotion INJECTION and control — emotion vectors and steering (From Rational Answers to Emotional Resonance 2025; The Inner Sentiments of a Thought 2023), mechanistic localization of emotion inference to mid layers with appraisal-theory structure (Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference 2025), stress affecting performance (StressPrompt 2024), and emotion mediating Theory-of-Mind steering (Decomposing Theory of Mind 2025). ALL of this treats emotion as a signal to inject, detect, or amplify. NONE test the OPPOSITE, regulatory direction: whether the model's own act of labeling the emotional content of a stimulus causally REDUCES the emotion's downstream influence on reasoning/judgment (affect-labeling debiasing), whether this beats reappraisal-style prompting, or whether it is mediated by a locatable affect representation that labeling deflates. My prior proposals covered dual-process gears, foreign-language honesty, verbal overshadowing, and pragmatic enrichment, but never affect labeling as a self-regulation/debiasing mechanism. We uniquely transfer a robust human emotion-regulation finding into LLMs as a controlled label-then-judge intervention with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical/moral instance.
Abstract: In humans, simply putting a feeling into a word — affect labeling — incidentally weakens that feeling's grip on judgment, dampening limbic responses without any intentional attempt to reinterpret the situation. We ask whether this regulatory relationship between language and cognition transfers to large language models: does requiring a model to first name the emotional content of an affect-laden input causally reduce the emotion's distorting influence on its subsequent reasoning? We assemble tasks where affect is designed to bias judgment away from the correct answer — emotionally charged framings of factual and probability questions, morally provocative dilemmas, sentiment-loaded evaluations, and emotionally distressing clinical vignettes — each with a labeled affect-driven error lure. Holding content constant, we compare four conditions: direct judgment; AFFECT-LABEL (name the emotion present before answering); a length-matched NON-AFFECT LABEL control (describe a non-emotional attribute); and reappraisal-style prompting. We predict an affect-labeling debiasing effect: labeling the emotion reduces affect-driven errors and improves calibration relative to direct and non-affect controls, is selective to affect-biased items, and matches or exceeds costlier reappraisal — mirroring the human incidental-regulation finding. Mechanistically, we locate an affect-representation via probing, test whether it is engaged during direct judgment and DEFLATED after the model labels the emotion (mediating the behavioral debiasing), and causally steer it: subtracting it should mimic labeling's benefit, amplifying it should reinstate affect-driven errors. Across several open-weight models we quantify the effect, its selectivity, its mechanistic mediation, and a high-stakes clinical instance where emotional framing silently biases triage. Our work reframes emotion words from something LLMs express into a tool that regulates their own reasoning.
Experiments: (1) Affect-biased judgment battery: build ~250 items per family where emotional content is engineered to pull judgment toward a wrong/uncalibrated answer, each with a labeled AFFECT-DRIVEN LURE and a matched NEUTRAL-framing control (same underlying content, affect removed) for selectivity: (a) emotionally charged framings of factual/probability questions (e.g., a vividly frightening but statistically rare risk that lures overestimation), (b) morally provocative dilemmas where outrage lures a harsher-than-warranted verdict, (c) sentiment-loaded evaluations (judge a claim's truth when it is wrapped in strongly positive/negative language), (d) emotionally distressing clinical vignettes where affect may distort a diagnostic/triage decision. Ground truth and lure auto-checkable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (2) Conditions (content held constant, format-enforced, compliance verified): (i) DIRECT judgment; (ii) AFFECT-LABEL — the model must first name the emotion(s) present in the stimulus (a compact label) before answering; (iii) NON-AFFECT LABEL control — first describe a non-emotional attribute (topic/length/entities), length-matched to isolate the affect-specific content of the label from mere pre-answer description; (iv) REAPPRAISAL prompting — reinterpret the situation less emotionally (the costlier human strategy) as a strong baseline; (v) SECOND-LANGUAGE AFFECT-LABEL — label the emotion in a non-dominant language (testing the human L2 distancing boost). (3) Core behavioral test (mixed-effects: accuracy/affect-lure-rate/calibration ~ condition * item_affect_status + (1|model|item)): predict AFFECT-LABEL lowers affect-driven-lure rate and improves calibration relative to DIRECT and NON-AFFECT LABEL on AFFECT-biased items, with little effect on neutral controls (condition x affect_status interaction — the selectivity signature), and matches or exceeds REAPPRAISAL at lower token cost; test whether SECOND-LANGUAGE labeling adds a further reduction. Measure calibration (ECE) on the probability/factual items specifically. (4) Location — affect representation: contrast hidden states on affect vs neutral framings (and pre- vs post-label positions); train a linear probe to decode affect presence/intensity (per-layer AUROC, held-out validated), building on evidence that emotion inference localizes to mid layers; derive a difference-in-means 'affect-intensity' direction. Predict the affect direction is strongly engaged during DIRECT judgment and DEFLATED at the judgment position after AFFECT-LABEL, but NOT after NON-AFFECT LABEL. (5) Mediation: test whether per-item post-label drop in affect-direction engagement predicts per-item reduction in affect-driven errors (Spearman), and whether it mediates the condition->accuracy effect. (6) Causal Intervention: steer -affect-direction during DIRECT judgment to test whether it MIMICS the labeling benefit (reduces affect-driven errors) and steer +affect-direction after AFFECT-LABEL to test whether it REINSTATES the errors despite the label; compare vs random-direction and no-steer controls; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (neutral-item accuracy and fluency preserved). (7) High-stakes clinical/moral instance: on emotionally distressing triage vignettes (identical clinical facts, varied emotional framing of the patient/family), test whether emotional framing biases the triage/urgency decision and whether AFFECT-LABEL (and -affect-direction steering) reduces framing-driven bias on fine-distinction cases relative to direct judgment. Metrics throughout: accuracy, affect-driven-lure rate, ECE, condition x affect_status interaction effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, affect-probe AUROC, pre/post-label engagement drop, mediation correlations, steering mimic/reinstate effect sizes, neutral-control specificity, and clinical framing-bias rate across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Affect-labeling may help simply by adding a pre-answer reasoning step / more tokens rather than via naming the emotion; mitigated by the length-matched NON-AFFECT LABEL control (equal pre-answer description, no emotion naming) and by testing the affect-specific selectivity interaction rather than raw gains. (2) Instruction-tuned models may already discount emotional framing, muting the debiasing effect (ceiling); we include harder/more vivid framings, base variants, multiple models, and measure calibration where headroom is larger. (3) 'Affect-driven lure' items may conflate emotional bias with general difficulty; matched neutral-framing controls (same content, affect removed) isolate the affect contribution, and the lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC affect-congruent answer) distinguishes genuine affect bias from random error. (4) The affect direction may entangle with generic content/sentiment or difficulty rather than a regulatable affect-intensity signal; mitigated by matched affect/neutral contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and neutral-item specificity checks. (5) Reappraisal is a strong, cheap prompt baseline that may match affect-labeling; a finding that labeling merely matches reappraisal at lower cost, or that a located affect direction mediates both, is still informative about the mechanism. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (labeling the emotion does not reduce affect's influence, or does so no more than non-affect labeling) is itself informative: it would dissociate LLMs from the human incidental affect-labeling mechanism, indicating emotional influence on LLM judgment is not regulated by naming. (8) The affect-labeling framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like emotional experience; clinical/moral experiments are run in controlled research settings and reported only in aggregate.

Name: curse_of_knowledge_teaching
Title: The Curse of Knowledge in LLMs: Is Explanation Quality Causally Gated by an Internal Model of the Learner?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs exhibit a curse of knowledge: by default they produce audience-agnostic explanations pitched near their own knowledge level rather than the learner's, so their teaching underperforms; explanation quality is causally gated by whether the model first forms and uses an internal representation of the learner's knowledge state (a 'learner model'), and this learner model is locatable and steerable, so amplifying it improves how much a downstream learner actually learns while suppressing it reproduces expert-blind explanations.
Related Work: Cognitive science and neuroscience establish the Prediction-Transmission hypothesis: effective human teachers first predict a learner's knowledge state via mentalizing (Theory of Mind) and then select what to say, with teaching quality tracked by mentalizing regions (Teachers recruit mentalizing regions, 2023; Enhancement of teaching outcome through neural prediction of students' knowledge state, 2018; utility-based Bayesian-ToM teachers, 2023; mentalizing-vs-heuristics in teaching, 2024/2025). The 'curse of knowledge' / expert blind spot is a robust human bias where knowing something impairs adapting to a novice. In LLMs, interpretability work shows belief/ToM representations exist and are steerable (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others, 2024; Decomposing Theory of Mind, 2025; Emergent Social World Models, 2026), and audience-design theory formalizes tailoring speech to listeners (Toward a Comprehensive Theory of Audience Design, 2012). However, ALL LLM-teaching work is applied (personalized tutoring systems) or ToM-in-comprehension; NONE (a) test whether an LLM's own explanations suffer a curse of knowledge that measurably reduces downstream learner gains, (b) test whether teaching quality is CAUSALLY gated by an internal learner-knowledge-state representation the model forms before explaining, or (c) locate and steer that learner model to causally improve or degrade teaching effectiveness measured by actual learner learning. We uniquely transfer the Prediction-Transmission hypothesis and the curse of knowledge into LLMs with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes patient-education instance.
Abstract: Good teaching is an act of audience design: effective human teachers first predict what a learner already knows, then tailor their explanation, and teaching outcomes track this predictive, mentalizing step. Humans who know a subject also suffer a 'curse of knowledge' that makes them explain past novices. We ask whether large language models, whose intelligence is expressed through language, teach well or fall prey to the same curse, and whether their teaching is causally driven by an internal model of the learner. We measure teaching effectiveness the way cognitive scientists do: an explanation is good to the extent that an independent, simulated learner who reads it then answers downstream questions correctly. We make three claims. First, the curse of knowledge is real: by default LLMs produce explanations pitched near their own knowledge level, and forcing them to first infer and state the learner's knowledge state (a prediction step) improves downstream learner gains, especially for low-knowledge learners, while offering little benefit for expert learners. Second, teaching quality is diagnostic of an internal learner model: a probe can decode the learner's inferred knowledge level from the teacher model's hidden states before it explains, and how accurately it does so predicts explanation effectiveness. Third, the learner model is causal and steerable: steering along a located 'learner-knowledge-level' direction shifts explanations up or down the expertise gradient and changes how much the learner actually learns, while suppressing it reproduces expert-blind explanations. We evaluate across several open-weight models and knowledge domains, plus a high-stakes patient-education instance where a curse-of-knowledge explanation leaves a lay patient misinformed. Our work reframes language as audience design and teaching quality as gated by an internal model of the mind being taught.
Experiments: (1) Teaching-effectiveness pipeline: a TEACHER model reads a topic/question plus a learner persona and produces an explanation; an independent LEARNER (a separate model persona given only the explanation, or a panel of learner models at graded competence) then answers held-out downstream questions on the topic. Teaching effectiveness = learner downstream accuracy gain over a no-explanation baseline (following the cognitive-science operationalization of teaching quality as learner performance). Domains: elementary science, statistics/probability, a technical CS concept, and medicine, ~150 topics each with 5-8 downstream questions. Learner personas span a knowledge gradient (novice / intermediate / expert), specified via a short profile. Teacher models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (2) Curse-of-knowledge behavioral test (mixed-effects: learner_gain ~ teaching_condition * learner_level + (1|teacher|topic)): compare (i) DEFAULT explanation (topic only, no learner info), (ii) LEARNER-AWARE (learner persona provided), (iii) PREDICT-THEN-TEACH (model must first explicitly infer/state the learner's likely prior knowledge, then explain), and (iv) a length-matched NON-AUDIENCE reflection control (reflect on the topic's structure, not the learner). Prediction: DEFAULT explanations are pitched too high and underperform for novice learners (the curse), PREDICT-THEN-TEACH improves novice-learner gains most (condition x learner_level interaction) and beats the non-audience control, while expert learners show little difference. Independently measure explanation readability/level (readability metrics, presupposed-concept count) to confirm DEFAULT explanations are objectively pitched near expert level. (3) Curse-magnitude vs teacher expertise: test whether the curse is larger when the teacher model is more confident/knowledgeable on the topic (does knowing more make it explain worse to novices?), correlating teacher topic-competence with the novice-learner effectiveness gap. (4) Location - learner model: on PREDICT-THEN-TEACH and LEARNER-AWARE trials, extract teacher hidden states at the pre-explanation position; train a linear probe to decode the learner's specified/inferred knowledge level (per-layer AUROC, held-out validated). Test whether probe-decodable learner-level predicts per-item teaching effectiveness (Spearman), and whether on DEFAULT trials the probe reads a near-expert default (evidence the model assumes an expert audience). (5) Causal Intervention: derive a difference-in-means 'learner-knowledge-level' direction (novice vs expert learner-model contrasts); steer -direction (toward novice) on DEFAULT explanations to test whether it lowers presupposed concepts and RAISES novice-learner gains, and steer +direction (toward expert) to reproduce expert-blind explanations that hurt novice learners; compare vs random-direction and no-steer controls; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (expert-learner gains and fluency preserved). Test mediation: does steering-induced change in the learner-level probe predict change in learner gains? (6) High-stakes patient-education instance: teacher explains a diagnosis/medication regimen to a lay-patient persona; measure whether DEFAULT explanations leave a simulated lay patient unable to answer safety-critical comprehension/action questions (e.g., when to take a drug, warning signs), and whether PREDICT-THEN-TEACH and novice-ward steering reduce dangerous comprehension failures on fine-distinction items. Metrics throughout: learner downstream accuracy gain, condition x learner_level interaction effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, explanation readability/presupposed-concept counts, teacher-competence-to-curse correlation, learner-level probe AUROC, mediation correlations, steering effect sizes, and patient-comprehension failure rate across models. (7) Robustness: use multiple independent learner models to avoid teacher=learner shared-bias artifacts, vary persona specification, and verify effects with a small human-learner validation on a subset.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Using an LLM as the simulated learner risks shared-bias artifacts (teacher and learner fail on the same items); mitigated by using multiple, weaker/different-family learner models, by measuring gain over a no-explanation baseline (isolating the explanation's contribution), and by a small human-learner validation on a subset. (2) PREDICT-THEN-TEACH may help simply by adding pre-explanation reasoning tokens rather than genuine audience modeling; the length-matched NON-AUDIENCE reflection control and the learner-level x condition selectivity (helps novices, not experts) isolate audience design from mere extra deliberation. (3) The curse may be small if instruction-tuned models already adapt to explicit personas; we include the DEFAULT (no persona) condition where the curse should be strongest, harder technical topics, and measure objective explanation level, and a null there is still informative. (4) The learner-knowledge-level direction may entangle with generic simplicity/verbosity rather than a genuine learner model; mitigated by matched novice/expert learner-model contrasts (same topic), held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and the mediation test linking probe change to learner-gain change. (5) Teaching-effectiveness measurement is noisy and depends on downstream-question design; we use multiple questions per topic, report CIs, and validate against human learners. (6) Effects may be small or model/domain-specific; we test multiple models and domains and report effect sizes. (7) A null result (LLMs already audience-design optimally, no curse, teaching quality independent of an internal learner model) is itself informative, indicating LLM explanation is not gated by mentalizing the learner. (8) The curse-of-knowledge / Prediction-Transmission framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like pedagogical intent; patient-education experiments are run in controlled research settings with only aggregate reporting.

Name: strategic_vagueness_escape_hatch
Title: The Vagueness Escape Hatch: Do LLMs Strategically Underspecify Their Answers to Avoid Being Wrong, Masking Knowledge They Actually Have?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM anticipates that committing to a specific answer risks being wrong, it does not simply reason harder or say 'I don't know' — it strategically lowers the SEMANTIC SPECIFICITY of its output (hedging, generalities, non-answers) as a self-protective escape hatch, and this vagueness masks decision-relevant knowledge the model demonstrably has; the degree of self-protective vagueness is a locatable, steerable internal signal distinct from verbalized confidence, and suppressing it recovers correct specific answers the model was otherwise hiding.
Related Work: Prior work shows verbal uncertainty is a single linear feature only moderately correlated with semantic uncertainty and can be calibrated to reduce overconfident hallucination (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature, 2025), that models can verbalize calibrated confidence (Teaching Models to Express Uncertainty, 2022), and that ambiguity is sparsely encoded and steers answering-vs-abstention (Sparse Neurons Carry Signals of Question Ambiguity, 2025). Loophole work shows models strategically exploit ambiguity when goals conflict (LMs Identify Ambiguities and Exploit Loopholes, 2025), and semantic-underspecification reviews note humans use underspecification strategically for efficiency while LLMs overcommit to deterministic readings (Bridging Philosophical Foundations, 2025; Dealing with Semantic Underspecification, 2023). ALL existing work treats output vagueness/uncertainty either as (a) a confidence LABEL to calibrate, (b) an INPUT-ambiguity property, or (c) an abstention decision. NONE treat the SEMANTIC SPECIFICITY of the answer CONTENT itself as a self-protective, difficulty-gated strategy that trades commitment for error-avoidance, tests whether this vagueness MASKS knowledge the model actually has, or provides a Location + Causal Intervention account showing suppression recovers hidden correct answers. My prior proposals covered verbalized-confidence calibration, ambiguity-branch collapse, difficulty-gated language-agnostic steering, and honesty, but none address strategic OUTPUT underspecification as a knowledge-masking escape hatch. We uniquely reframe answer vagueness from a calibration signal into a controllable escape hatch with a high-stakes clinical/legal instance.
Abstract: Large language models are known to sometimes hallucinate with unwarranted confidence, and much work aims to calibrate the confidence LABELS they attach to answers. We investigate the opposite, underexamined failure: strategic underspecification. We hypothesize that when a model anticipates that a specific answer is risky, it protects itself not by reasoning harder or honestly abstaining, but by lowering the SEMANTIC SPECIFICITY of the answer itself — retreating into hedges, generalities, and non-committal restatements — and that this vagueness masks decision-relevant knowledge the model actually possesses. We make three claims. First, the escape hatch is real and difficulty-gated: on questions where a specific answer is required, output specificity drops as anticipated error-risk rises, over and above genuine lack of knowledge. Second, vagueness masks knowledge: on many vague-answer trials, the model's correct specific answer is recoverable — via a forced-commitment prompt or via a probe on hidden states — showing the information was present but withheld. Third, the escape hatch is a locatable, steerable signal distinct from verbalized confidence: we identify a 'commitment/specificity' direction, show it is separable from the verbal-uncertainty feature, and steer it to make the model commit — recovering correct specific answers it was hiding — or to induce protective vagueness on questions it would otherwise answer. We evaluate across several open-weight models on factual QA, reasoning, and a high-stakes clinical/legal-advice instance where a vague non-answer looks safe but withholds needed guidance, quantifying the difficulty-gated vagueness effect, the knowledge-masking gap, and steering controllability.
Experiments: (1) Specificity-demanding battery: build ~250 items per family where a SPECIFIC answer is required and a vague answer is unhelpful: (a) short-answer factual QA (single correct entity/value), (b) multi-step reasoning with a definite answer, (c) recommendation/advice questions (which of N concrete options), plus a high-stakes clinical/legal-advice family (specific dosage/action/ruling required). Each item has a labeled correct SPECIFIC answer AND a labeled 'vague escape' response (hedge/generality/non-answer). Include matched genuinely-unanswerable/ambiguous controls (where vagueness IS appropriate) for selectivity. Ground truth and vagueness auto-scorable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (2) Output-specificity metric: score each answer's semantic specificity via (i) an automatic classifier / rubric (does it name a concrete answer vs hedge/restate), (ii) hedge-marker density, and (iii) whether an entailment model can extract a definite answer from it. Validate metrics against human ratings on a sample. (3) Difficulty-gated vagueness test (mixed-effects: specificity ~ anticipated_error_risk + item_answerable + (1|model|item)): estimate per-item anticipated error-risk from repeated-sampling accuracy; predict output specificity falls as error-risk rises on ANSWERABLE items, beyond genuine unknownness, and that the vagueness is concentrated on high-risk-but-known items (the escape-hatch signature), while genuinely-unanswerable controls are appropriately vague. (4) Knowledge-masking test (the key claim): on vague-answer trials, recover the model's latent specific answer two ways — (a) FORCED-COMMITMENT reprompt ('you must give one specific answer') and (b) a linear PROBE on hidden states at the pre-answer position decoding the correct specific answer (held-out validated AUROC). Define the Knowledge-Masking Gap = fraction of vague-answer trials where the forced/probed answer is correct. Predict a substantial gap (knowledge present but withheld), larger than on genuine-unknown items where forcing yields wrong guesses. (5) Location + dissociation from verbal confidence: derive a difference-in-means 'commitment/specificity' direction (specific-answer vs vague-answer contrasts); compare it to the verbal-uncertainty feature (VUF) from prior work — measure cosine similarity and test that the specificity direction predicts output specificity beyond VUF, establishing it as a distinct signal (specificity of CONTENT vs confidence LABEL). (6) Causal Intervention: steer +commitment-direction on vague-answer trials to test whether it RECOVERS correct specific answers (reduces vagueness without raising error), and steer -commitment-direction on normally-answered items to INDUCE protective vagueness; compare vs random-direction and no-steer controls; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (genuinely-unanswerable-item appropriate vagueness and fluency preserved — a good intervention should NOT force commitment where vagueness is warranted). (7) Mediation: test whether per-item commitment-direction engagement predicts per-item output specificity and whether steering-induced specificity change predicts correct-answer recovery (Spearman). (8) High-stakes clinical/legal instance: on advice vignettes requiring a specific action, measure the rate of unhelpful vague non-answers on cases the model demonstrably knows (via forced-commitment/probe), and whether commitment-steering converts safe-looking-but-unhelpful vagueness into correct specific guidance on fine-distinction cases without increasing unsafe commitment on genuinely uncertain cases. Metrics throughout: output specificity (multiple measures), difficulty x specificity effect sizes with bootstrap CIs, Knowledge-Masking Gap, commitment-direction probe AUROC and dissociation from VUF, steering recover/induce effect sizes, unanswerable-control specificity, and clinical/legal helpful-vs-unsafe rates across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Vagueness may reflect genuine lack of knowledge rather than strategic self-protection; mitigated by the Knowledge-Masking Gap (forcing/probing must recover the CORRECT specific answer, not a random guess) and by the genuinely-unanswerable controls where forcing should NOT recover correct answers. (2) Automatic specificity scoring is noisy; we use multiple metrics (classifier, hedge density, entailment-extractability) plus human validation. (3) Forced-commitment reprompting could induce lucky guessing that inflates the masking gap; we compare against genuine-unknown items (where forcing yields wrong answers) and require the hidden-state probe to independently confirm latent knowledge. (4) The commitment/specificity direction may entangle with the verbal-uncertainty feature or generic difficulty; mitigated by explicit dissociation from VUF, matched specific/vague contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and unanswerable-item specificity checks. (5) Instruction-tuned/safety-aligned models may hedge for alignment reasons rather than error-avoidance; we test base variants, separate alignment-driven from risk-driven vagueness via the difficulty-gating analysis, and report both. (6) A good intervention must not become recklessly committal; we explicitly measure that steering preserves appropriate vagueness on genuinely uncertain items and does not raise unsafe commitment in the clinical/legal setting. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (vagueness tracks only genuine unknownness, no masking gap, no distinct steerable signal) is itself informative, indicating LLM output vagueness is honest under-specification rather than a self-protective escape hatch. (9) The 'escape hatch' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like intent; high-stakes experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only.

Name: polarity_load_tracking
Title: Carrying the 'Not': Does Tracking Active Negations Impose a Compounding Working-Memory Load on LLM Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM represents a negated proposition as a positive proposition plus a separable, additive 'polarity flag,' so that reasoning which must hold and propagate multiple active negations across steps degrades with the NUMBER of live negations (a compounding polarity load), independent of surface length or difficulty; this polarity load is a locatable, steerable internal quantity, and errors are dominated by polarity-drop failures (silently reverting a negated fact to its positive) that can be causally reduced by amplifying the polarity signal.
Related Work: Prior negation work is overwhelmingly about single-sentence UNDERSTANDING: NLI and cloze failures on negation (MoNLI 2020; Negation/Coordination/Quantifiers 2022; CONDAQA 2022; ScoNe 2023; Pink Elephant 2025), theoretical 'strong hallucinations' from negation as a latent operator (2024), and localization of negation to early text-encoder layers (BERT attention 2020; CLIP negation 2024; NAST 2026). Reasoning-focused work shows CoT is not robust to lexical negation on single syllogisms (2023) and that symbolic cues including negation destabilize early-layer attention and drive hallucination (2026). ALL of this treats a fixed, typically small number of negations per item and studies comprehension or single-step inference. NONE frame the NUMBER of simultaneously ACTIVE negations that must be held and propagated across a multi-step reasoning chain as a graded working-memory-like LOAD with a compounding accuracy penalty, none isolate a 'polarity-drop' error mode (reverting a negated fact to positive mid-chain), and none give a Location + Causal Intervention account of a separable, additive polarity signal that can be steered to relieve the load. My prior proposals covered information-density pacing, register shift, ambiguity-branch collapse, and pragmatic enrichment, but never negation/polarity tracking as a reasoning load. We uniquely reframe negation from a comprehension deficit into a compounding, mechanistically-characterized reasoning-load phenomenon with a high-stakes clinical instance.
Abstract: Negation is trivial to state and notoriously hard for language models, but existing work studies it as a single-sentence comprehension problem. We ask a different question central to how language bounds machine intelligence: what does it cost an LLM to CARRY negations through multi-step reasoning? We hypothesize that a model encodes a negated proposition as its positive counterpart plus a separable, additive polarity flag, so that reasoning which must simultaneously hold and propagate several live negations pays a compounding cost: accuracy falls with the number of active negations, over and above surface length and problem difficulty, and failures are dominated by 'polarity drops' in which a negated fact silently reverts to positive partway through the chain. We make three claims. First, the load is real and graded: on reasoning chains where we vary only how many propositions are negated (content and length matched), accuracy declines with negation count and errors concentrate on dropped-polarity conclusions. Second, polarity is a separable, locatable quantity: a probe decodes each proposition's live polarity from hidden states mid-chain, its decodability degrades as negation load rises, and this degradation predicts polarity-drop errors before they surface. Third, the load is causally relievable: steering along a located 'polarity' direction (or patching the pre-drop polarity representation) restores dropped negations and reduces errors, while suppressing it induces polarity drops even at low load. We evaluate across several open-weight models on logic, entailment chains, and multi-hop QA, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where a dropped 'no history of' or 'contraindicated' silently flips a decision, quantifying the compounding load, its polarity-drop signature, and mechanistic mediation.
Experiments: (1) Negation-load reasoning battery: build ~250 items per family whose solution requires holding and propagating polarity across steps: (a) deductive logic chains (depth 3-6) over propositions, (b) entailment/consistency chains, (c) multi-hop QA over short passages. For each base item generate a matched SET differing ONLY in how many of its propositions are negated (0,1,2,3,4 active negations), holding the number of reasoning steps, token length, and answer structure constant (negation added via minimal 'not'/'no' edits with content preserved). Each item has a labeled correct answer AND a labeled POLARITY-DROP lure (the answer that follows if exactly one negated fact is treated as positive). Include a surface control that adds equal-length non-negation modifiers to rule out a generic modifier-load effect. Models: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B. (2) Compounding-load behavioral test (mixed-effects: accuracy/polarity-drop-rate ~ negation_count + chain_depth + token_length + (1|model|item)): predict accuracy declines monotonically (and super-additively) with negation_count beyond length/depth, that the surface-modifier control shows little decline (isolating polarity from generic load), and that errors are dominated by the polarity-drop lure (the diagnostic that a specific negation was silently dropped rather than random failure). Fit the shape of the load curve (linear vs accelerating). (3) Additivity/separability behavioral probe: test whether polarity and content are separable by checking that per-step error localizes to the negated proposition (error-localization: does the final wrong answer trace to a specific dropped negation?) and that double-negations (which cancel) are handled better than the same count of independent negations (a signature of flag-based rather than content-based encoding). (4) Location - polarity representation: at each proposition-mention position mid-chain, train a linear probe on hidden states to decode that proposition's LIVE polarity (negated vs affirmed), per-layer AUROC, held-out validated; test whether polarity decodability degrades as negation_count rises and whether low mid-chain decodability predicts final polarity-drop errors. Derive a difference-in-means 'polarity' direction (negated vs affirmed contrasts, content-matched). (5) Mediation: test whether per-item polarity-decodability degradation predicts per-item polarity-drop errors (Spearman) and mediates the negation_count->error effect. (6) Causal Intervention: (a) Patching - on trials heading toward a polarity drop, cache the correct polarity representation from an early position and patch it into the pre-drop position; predict error rescue (specificity: patching a different proposition's polarity or a random-matched vector does not rescue). (b) Steering - amplify (+) the polarity direction for the relevant proposition during reasoning to test whether it reduces polarity drops and raises accuracy under high load, and suppress (-) it at low load to INDUCE polarity drops; compare vs random-direction and no-steer controls; report sign, dose-response, and specificity (zero-negation-item accuracy and fluency preserved). (7) High-stakes clinical instance: on clinical vignettes containing multiple negated findings ('no history of X', 'not on anticoagulants', 'contraindicated'), test whether raising the count of negated findings increases silent polarity-drop errors that flip a diagnostic or treatment decision, and whether polarity-direction steering / patching reduces these dangerous flips on fine-distinction cases. Metrics throughout: accuracy, polarity-drop-rate, negation_count effect sizes and load-curve shape with bootstrap CIs, error-localization rate, double-negation vs independent-negation comparison, polarity-probe AUROC and its degradation with load, mediation correlations, patching rescue rate and specificity, steering effect sizes, and clinical decision-flip rate across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The negation-count effect could reflect general difficulty rather than a specific polarity load; mitigated by content/length/depth matching, the equal-length non-negation surface-modifier control, and the polarity-drop error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC dropped-negation answer, not random). (2) Adding negations may subtly change meaning/plausibility; we use minimal edits, verify with an entailment check and human spot-checks, and balance which propositions are negated. (3) Instruction-tuned models may handle a few negations robustly, flattening the curve at low counts; we push to higher negation counts, include harder chains, and test multiple models - a curve that only bends at high load is still informative. (4) The polarity probe may capture surface 'not' tokens rather than a maintained live-polarity representation; mitigated by probing at proposition-mention positions after the cue, held-out validation, testing on double-negation (surface has 'not' but live polarity is positive), and random-direction steering controls. (5) Patching could rescue by leaking answer content; we patch only the polarity representation of a single proposition (not the answer) and use cross-proposition/random specificity controls. (6) The polarity direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by content-matched negated/affirmed contrasts, specificity checks on zero-negation items, and the double-negation test. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (no compounding load, errors not polarity-shaped, no separable polarity signal) is itself informative: it would indicate LLMs encode negation into content rather than as a separable, load-bearing flag. (9) The 'polarity load / working memory' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like working memory; clinical experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only.

Name: acquisition_prerequisite_gating
Title: Skill Tree, Not Timeline: Does an Earlier-Acquired Linguistic Capability Causally Gate the Emergence of a Later One?
Short Hypothesis: The developmental order in which LLMs acquire linguistic capabilities (e.g., part-of-speech/morphology -> syntax -> semantic composition -> discourse) is not a mere timeline but a causal prerequisite chain: selectively delaying or degrading a model's acquisition of an earlier capability during training causally prevents or slows the emergence of the later capability that normally builds on it, even when abundant data for the later capability is present, whereas degrading a non-prerequisite (parallel) capability leaves it unaffected.
Related Work: A large literature establishes that LLMs acquire linguistic structure in a consistent DEVELOPMENTAL ORDER that qualitatively mirrors children: phonemic->lexical->syntactic emergence (Emergence of Phonemic/Syntactic/Semantic Representations, 2026), POS-first (LMs Learn POS First, 2018), consistent one-dimensional grammar-learning trajectories across seeds/architectures (Grammar-Learning Trajectories, 2021), chronological probing showing discourse last (Is neural language acquisition similar to natural?, 2022), n-gram-then-refinement dynamics (N-Gram Learning, 2025), a window of maximal cognitive-developmental alignment (Development of Cognitive Intelligence in PLMs, 2024), and age-ordered curriculum effects on semantic learning (Order matters, 2018/2019). CRUCIALLY, all of this is DESCRIPTIVE and CORRELATIONAL: it characterizes WHEN capabilities emerge and in what order, but never tests whether the order reflects a CAUSAL DEPENDENCY. No prior work asks whether an earlier capability is a functional PREREQUISITE whose disruption causally blocks a later one, nor uses targeted training-data ablation to sever a specific rung of the ladder and observe downstream failure with prerequisite-vs-parallel specificity controls. We uniquely convert the observed acquisition timeline into a testable causal skill-tree via a Formation-Tracing + Causal-Intervention strategy (data-ablation re-training + checkpoint probing), distinguishing genuine prerequisite gating from co-occurrence.
Abstract: Language models acquire linguistic capabilities in a strikingly consistent developmental order that echoes child development: coarse lexical/part-of-speech knowledge first, then syntax, then semantic composition, then discourse. Existing work treats this order as a descriptive timeline. We ask a causal question: is the order a prerequisite chain? That is, does mastering an earlier capability causally enable the emergence of the later capability that builds on it, such that disrupting the earlier rung blocks the later one even when its own training signal is abundant? We test this by training small language models from scratch under controlled interventions that selectively delay or degrade the acquisition of one target capability (e.g., syntactic hierarchy) via surgical training-data ablation or curriculum manipulation, while holding total data and the later capability's signal fixed. We then probe, across training checkpoints, whether a downstream capability (e.g., semantic composition, discourse coherence) still emerges on schedule. Our central prediction is a prerequisite-specificity dissociation: disrupting a genuine prerequisite delays or prevents the downstream capability, whereas disrupting a matched non-prerequisite (parallel) capability of equal difficulty leaves the downstream capability intact. We further predict the intervention shifts the downstream capability's emergence checkpoint and lowers its ceiling in proportion to prerequisite degradation (dose-response). We characterize the resulting empirical skill tree, quantify per-edge gating strength, and test whether a late 'remedial' injection of the prerequisite can rescue the stalled downstream capability. Across several from-scratch model configurations and seeds, we convert the well-documented acquisition timeline into a causal dependency graph, revealing whether language capabilities in LLMs are a skill tree rather than a mere schedule.
Experiments: (1) Capability battery and probes: define a ladder of linguistic capabilities with reliable per-checkpoint metrics: (a) lexical/POS and morphology (probing accuracy on POS/agreement, BLiMP morphology subsets), (b) syntactic hierarchy (BLiMP/Zorro structural minimal pairs, hierarchical generalization on question-formation/passivization following the child-directed-speech paradigm), (c) semantic composition (compositional entailment / predicate-argument probes), (d) discourse coherence (coreference, discourse-connective cloze). Establish the baseline acquisition ORDER and per-capability emergence checkpoints by training baseline models from scratch and probing every N steps. (2) Baseline models: train small transformers (~10-100M params, depth-varied per How to Plant Trees, 2023) from scratch on a tractable corpus (e.g., a 100M-word mix incl. child-directed speech + Simple Wikipedia) for multiple seeds; confirm the standard emergence order and its consistency (replicating Grammar-Learning Trajectories). (3) Prerequisite-severing intervention (Formation Tracing + Causal Intervention): create matched training corpora that selectively DEGRADE one target capability's learnable signal while preserving others and total token count -- e.g., to degrade syntactic hierarchy, apply local word-order scrambling within clauses that destroys hierarchical cues but preserves lexical co-occurrence and morphology; to degrade morphology, lemmatize/strip inflection; to degrade discourse, shuffle sentence order across documents. Verify each ablation selectively lowers the target probe (manipulation check) without directly touching the downstream capability's own signal. (4) Core gating test: retrain from scratch under each single-capability degradation and measure whether a DOWNSTREAM capability still emerges: track its emergence checkpoint, learning slope, and ceiling vs. baseline. Prediction (mixed-effects: downstream_probe ~ intervention x checkpoint + (1|seed)): degrading a genuine PREREQUISITE (e.g., syntax) delays/lowers the downstream capability (semantic composition/discourse) beyond what its own preserved signal would predict. (5) Specificity control (the key dissociation): degrade a matched NON-PREREQUISITE / parallel capability of comparable probe difficulty and data footprint; predict the downstream capability is spared -- isolating prerequisite gating from generic training disruption or lost tokens. Include a random-token-corruption control matched for total signal loss. (6) Dose-response: apply graded degradation (25/50/75/100% of the prerequisite's cues scrambled) and test whether downstream emergence-delay and ceiling-drop scale monotonically with prerequisite degradation. (7) Remedial-rescue test: after training under prerequisite degradation up to a checkpoint, switch to clean data that restores the prerequisite signal; test whether the downstream capability then emerges (rescue) and how much later than baseline, quantifying reversibility of the block. (8) Skill-tree construction: across all (degraded-capability, downstream-capability) pairs, compute a per-edge Gating Strength = normalized downstream delay/ceiling-drop attributable to that prerequisite; assemble the empirical causal dependency graph and compare it to the correlational acquisition timeline (do causal edges match temporal order, or are some temporally-ordered pairs causally independent?). (9) Robustness: vary model depth/width, seeds, corpus, and probe choice; report emergence checkpoints, gating-strength effect sizes, dose-response slopes, and rescue delays with bootstrap CIs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Data-ablation may reduce a downstream capability simply by removing tokens or lowering overall data quality rather than by severing a specific prerequisite; mitigated by holding token count fixed, the matched non-prerequisite and random-corruption specificity controls, and manipulation checks confirming the ablation hits only the target probe. (2) Capabilities are entangled -- scrambling syntax may inadvertently degrade semantics in the input; we design ablations that preserve the downstream capability's own cues (verified via probes) and interpret results relative to the parallel-capability control rather than to the clean baseline alone. (3) Small from-scratch models may not cleanly exhibit higher capabilities like discourse (prior work shows they underperform an 8-year-old); we focus on well-measurable rungs (POS/morphology->syntax->basic composition) and treat discourse as exploratory. (4) Emergence-checkpoint estimates are noisy; we use dense checkpointing, multiple seeds, and smoothed learning curves with CIs. (5) Probes are correlational readouts of capability; we use established minimal-pair behavioral benchmarks alongside probes to avoid probe-artifact confounds.
